The '''Medical College Admission Test''' ('''MCAT'''; {{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɛ|m|k|æ|t}} {{respell|EM|kat}}) is a [[Computer-based testing|computer-based]] [[standardized examination]] for prospective [[medical students]] in the [[United States]], [[Canada]], [[Australia]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Melbourne Medical School International Applicants |url=http://medicine.unimelb.edu.au/study-here/doctor_of_medicine/application_process/international |website=University of Melbourne |access-date=23 October 2015}}</ref> and the [[Offshore medical school|Caribbean Islands]]. It is designed to assess [[problem solving]], critical thinking, written analysis and knowledge of scientific concepts and principles. Before 2007, the exam was a paper-and-pencil test; since 2007, all administrations of the exam have been computer-based.

The most recent version of the exam was introduced in April 2015 and takes approximately {{Fraction|7|1|2}} hours to complete, including breaks. The test is scored in a range from 472 to 528. The MCAT is administered by the [[Association of American Medical Colleges]] (AAMC).<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/applying-medical-school/taking-mcat-exam/ |title=Taking the MCAT® Exam |website=Association of American Medical Colleges |access-date=2019-07-23}}</ref>

== History ==

=== Moss Test: 1928–1946 ===
In the 1920s, dropout rates in US medical schools soared from 5% to 50%,<ref name="Journal">{{Cite journal |author=McGaghie, William C. |title=Assessing Readiness for Medical Education |journal=[[Journal of the American Medical Association]] |volume=288 |issue=9 |pages=1085–1090 |date=2002-09-04 |pmid=12204076 |doi=10.1001/jama.288.9.1085}}</ref> leading to the development of a test that would measure readiness for medical school. [[Physician]] and psychologist [[Fred August Moss]] and his colleagues developed the "Scholastic Aptitude Test for Medical Students" consisting of true-false and multiple choice questions divided into six to eight subtests. Topics tested included [[visual memory]], memory for content, scientific vocabulary, scientific definitions, understanding of printed material, premedical information, and logical reasoning. The score scale varied from different test forms. Though it had been criticized at the time for testing only memorization ability and thus only readiness for the first two years of medical school, later scholars{{Who|date=June 2017}} denied this. In addition to stricter medical school admission procedures and higher educational standards, the national dropout rate among freshman medical students decreased from 20% in 1925–1930 to 7% in 1946.<ref>{{cite book |title=In the Nation's Compelling Interest: Ensuring Diversity in the Health-Care Workforce |chapter=Reconceptualizing Admissions Policies and Practices |editor-last1=Smedley |editor-first1=BD |editor-last2=Stith Butler |editor-first2=A |editor-last3=Bristow |editor-first3=LR |year=2004 |publisher=National Academies Press (US) |location=Washington, DC |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK216012/}}</ref>

=== A simpler test: 1946–1962 ===
Advancements in test measurement technology, including machine scoring of tests, and changed views regarding test scores and medical school readiness reflected the evolution of the test in this period. The test underwent three major changes. It now had only four sub tests, including verbal ability, quantitative ability, science achievement, and understanding modern society. Questions were all in multiple-choice format. Each subtest was given a single score, and the total score was derived from the sum of the scores from the subtests. The total score ranged from 200 to 800. The individual scores helped medical school admission committees to differentiate the individual abilities among their candidates. Admission committees, however, did not consider the "understanding modern society" section to be of great importance, even though it was created to reward those with broad liberal arts skills, which included knowledge of history, government, economics, and sociology. Committees placed greater emphasis on scores on the scientific achievement section as it was a better predictor of performance in medical school.{{cn|date=October 2023}}

From 1946 to 1948, the test was called the "Professional School Aptitude Test" before finally changing its name to the "Medical College Admission Test" when the developer of the test, the Graduate Record Office (under contract with the [[Association of American Medical Colleges|AAMC]]) merged with the newly formed [[Educational Testing Service]] (ETS). In 1960, the AAMC transferred its contract over to [[Harcourt Assessment|The Psychological Corporation]], which was then in charge of maintaining and developing the test.{{Citation needed|date=May 2020}}

=== Status quo: 1962–1977 ===
From 1962 to 1977, the MCAT retained much of its previous format, though the "understanding modern society" section was renamed as "general information" due to its expanded content. Handbooks at the time criticized the test as only a measure of intellectual achievement and not of personal characteristics expected of physicians. Admission committees responded to this criticism by measuring personal characteristics among their applicants with various approaches.{{cn|date=October 2023}}

=== Phase four: 1977–1991 ===
During phase four, the MCAT underwent several changes. The "general information" section was eliminated and a broader range of knowledge was tested. At this point, topics tested included scientific knowledge, science problems, reading skills analysis, and quantitative skills analysis. Individual scores were reported for biology, chemistry, and physics rather than a composite science score, thus six different scores for the whole test were reported. The score scale changed to 1–15 as opposed to 200–800 from previous versions of the test. Cultural and social bias was minimized. Though the AAMC claimed the new version intended to evaluate "information gathering and analysis, discerning and formulating relationships, and other problem-solving skills", no research supported this claim.

=== Changes: 1991–2014 ===
In 1991, the test changed again. Though the test was still divided into four subtests, they were renamed as the verbal reasoning, biological sciences, physical sciences, and writing sample sections. Questions retained the multiple-choice format, though the majority of the questions were divided into passage sets. Passage-based questions were implemented to evaluate "text comprehension, data analysis, ability to evaluate an argument, or apply knowledge from the passage to other contexts." A new scoring scale was also implemented. The total composite score, which had a range of 3–45, was based on the individual scores of the verbal reasoning, biological sciences, and physical sciences, which each had a score range of 1–15. The writing sample, which consisted of two essays to be written within 30 minutes for each, was graded on a letter scale of J–T with T being the highest attainable score.{{cn|date=October 2023}}

The exam in this format was available twice a year (April and August), lasted 8-9 hours with a lunch break, and consisted of 214 questions in addition to the essays. It took 60 days for students to receive their score.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kaptest.com/oneoff/mcat-test-change/computer-based-mcat-information.jhtml |title=What is changing on the MCAT? |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928163708/http://www.kaptest.com/oneoff/mcat-test-change/computer-based-mcat-information.jhtml |archive-date=2007-09-28 |website=Kaplan Test}}</ref>
On July 18, 2005, the AAMC announced that it would offer the paper-and-pencil version of the MCAT only through August 2006. A subset of testing sites offered a computer-based version of the full-length exam throughout 2005 and 2006.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aamc.org/newsroom/pressrel/2005/050718.htm |title=Medical College Admission Test Will Convert to Computer-Based Format |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927215420/http://www.aamc.org/newsroom/pressrel/2005/050718.htm |archive-date=2007-09-27 |website=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref>

=== MR5 and the 2015 test ===
The MR5 advisory committee was appointed by AAMC in fall 2008 to conduct the fifth comprehensive review of the MCAT exam and to recommend changes for the new exam set to be released in 2015.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |url=https://www.aamc.org/download/273766/data/finalmr5recommendations.pdf |title=Final MR5 Recommendations |website=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref> The advisory committee had 21 members including medical school deans and administrators, basic and clinical science faculty, pre-health advisors, one medical student and a medical resident.<ref name=":02" /> The recommendations determined were also based on responses from 2,700 surveys, over 75 meetings and conferences, and 90 outreach events to solicit input.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.abe.wildapricot.org/Resources/Documents/MR5%20Comprehensive%20Review%20of%20MCAT%20March%202011%20e-Newsletter.docx |title=MR5: 5th Comprehensive Review of the Medical College Admission Test® March 2011 e-newsletter}}</ref> The recommendations considered the content and format of the MCAT, the resources that should be provided relating to the exam, and the changes that should be made to medical school admissions in general.<ref name=":02" />
[[File:MR5 Science Topics Survey.jpg|thumb|490x490px|Ratings of the Importance of Natural and Behavioral Sciences Topics for Mastery of Future Medical School Curricula<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |url=http://www.abe.wildapricot.org/Resources/Documents/MR5%20Ratings%20of%20the%20Importance%20of%20Topics%20in%20Success%20in%20Medical%20School.pdf |title=Ratings of the Importance of Topics in the Natural Sciences, Research Methods, Statistics, and Behavioral Sciences to Success in Medical School |publisher=Wild Apricot}}</ref>]]
To determine the content that should be tested for the exam, the MR5 committee surveyed medical school faculty, residents, and medical students, and asked what concepts entering students need to know to be successful in medical school curricula.<ref name=":12" /> Three separate surveys were sent asking about concepts in the natural sciences, research methods, and behavioral sciences. The MR5 committee also consulted various expert committees from within and beyond the AAMC.

The largest changes in the exam consist of testing in biochemistry, psychology and sociology concepts. The addition of biochemistry material follows survey results placing biochemistry concepts as highest importance for success in future medical school curricula.<ref name=":12" /> The addition of behavioral and cultural material was recommended to provide a solid foundation for learning of these concepts in medical school. According to the committee, psychological science should be understood by medical students as an essential aspect of healthcare.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.apa.org/ed/precollege/ptn/2012/08/mcat.aspx |title=The teaching of psychology and the new MCAT |website=apa.org |language=en |access-date=2018-04-14}}</ref> The writing sample section was also removed, since data showed that these scores were not used by most admission committees.<ref name=":02" /> These changes were revealed in 2012 so that undergraduate premedical advisers studied the MR5 documents to translate tested core competencies into premedical course recommendations at their campuses.<ref name=":02" />

This version of the MCAT has been administered since March 2015 and is expected to be in place until 2030.<ref name=":1" />

== Administration ==
The exam is offered 25 or more times per year at [[Pearson VUE]] centers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://home.pearsonvue.com/About-Pearson-VUE/Press-Room/2017/Pearson-VUE-to-deliver-MCAT®-beginning-in-2018.aspx |title=Pearson VUE to deliver Medical College Admission Test® (MCAT®) beginning in 2018 |year=2017 |publisher=Pearson VUE}}</ref> The number of administrations may vary each year. As of the 2023 MCAT testing period, 41.8% of students take the MCAT within one year of graduation, 32% sit the exam within 1-2 years post-graduation, 13.5% take the exam between three and four years after graduation and 12.7% sit for the exam five or more years after graduation.<ref>{{cite report |title=Post-MCAT Questionnaire 2023 Report |author=Association of American Medical Colleges |year=2023 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges |url=https://www.aamc.org/media/75031/download}}</ref>

The test, updated in 2015, consists of four sections, listed in the order that they are administered
* '''Chemical and Physical Foundations of Biological Systems'''
* '''Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills (CARS)'''
* '''Biological and Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems'''
* '''Psychological, Social and Biological Foundations of Behavior'''

The four sections are in multiple-choice format. The passages and questions are predetermined, and thus do not change significantly in difficulty depending on the performance of the test taker (unlike, for example, the general [[Graduate Record Examinations]]). To account for slight differences in difficulty across test versions, the exam uses a scaled score for each section, converting numerical scores to a scaled score between 118 and 132 per section.<ref>{{cite web |title=How is the MCAT Exam Scored? |year=2024 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/mcat-scores/how-mcat-exam-scored}}</ref>

== Test structure ==
[[File:MCAT Sections with Subjects Percentage and College Prerequisites.jpg|alt=MCAT Sections with Subjects Percentage and College Prerequisites|thumb|A detailed overview of the Medical College Admission Test (MCAT). It outlines the four sections, number of questions, duration, subject percentages, and helpful college courses. It includes the highest possible and average total scores. Source: [https://www.mcat-prep.com/what-is-the-mcat/ MCAT-prep.com]]]

The MCAT consists of four distinct sections that are individually scored. Each section is allotted either 90 or 95 minutes and tests between 53 and 59 questions.<ref>{{cite report |title=What's on the MCAT Exam? |year=2020 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/media/9261/download}}</ref> Including breaks, the full examination lasts approximately {{Fraction|7|1|2}} hours.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |url=https://aamc-orange.global.ssl.fastly.net/production/media/filer_public/c3/de/c3de3536-7c7b-4318-99cc-431376ec23dc/essentials_2018_final_feb2018.pdf |title=The MCAT® Essentials for Testing Year 2018 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref> The information for each of the science sections is organized into 10 foundational concepts and four Scientific Inquiry & Reasoning Skills.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/applying-medical-school/article/whats-mcat-exam/ |title=What's on the MCAT Exam? |access-date=2018-03-30 |language=en |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref> The science passages are guided by Scientific Reasoning and Inquiry Skills identified by the MR5 for medical school success.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |url=https://members.aamc.org/eweb/upload/Final%20Recommendation%20for%20the%202015%20MCAT%20Exam%20ANN11-589.pdf |title=Final Recommendations for the 2015 MCAT Exam |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref> The Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section focuses on three skills, since this section does not require outside knowledge to answer questions.<ref name="students-residents.aamc.org">{{Cite news |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/applying-medical-school/article/mcat-2015-cars-overview/ |title=Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills Section: Overview |access-date=2018-03-30 |language=en |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref>

=== Chemical and Physical Foundations of Biological Systems ===
This section tests chemistry and physics in the scope of biological systems, requiring understanding of organic and inorganic chemistry and physics as well as biology and biochemistry. Specifically, this section focuses on the physical principles underlying biological processes and chemical interactions that form the basis of a broader understanding of living systems. Understanding of research methods and statistics are also important to successfully reason through this material.<ref name=":0" />

=== Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills (CARS) ===
The CARS section is similar to verbal reasoning sections providing passages with questions testing [[reading comprehension]]. The 500-to-600-word passages can cover topics ranging from the social sciences to the humanities, sometimes presenting in a convoluted or biased manner requiring the reader to consider what is being written from multiple perspectives.<ref name="students-residents.aamc.org" /> The passages are designed to discuss topics that are unfamiliar to the reader, but success in this section requires strictly using information from the passage without using previously known knowledge.<ref>{{Citation |title=CARS overview |url=https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/critical-analysis-and-reasoning-skills-practice-questions/critical-analysis-and-reasoning-skills-tutorial/v/cars-overview |language=en |access-date=2018-03-30 |publisher=Khan Academy}}</ref>

=== Biological and Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems ===
This section mainly tests biology and biochemistry but also requires an understanding of organic and inorganic chemistry. Students will have to answer questions about the functions of biomolecules, processes unique to living organisms, and the organization of biological systems. Understanding of research methods and statistics are also important to successfully reason through this material.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://aamc-orange.global.ssl.fastly.net/production/media/filer_public/f8/bc/f8bcec72-4ac3-4e5a-8c27-631d2096c569/combined_mcat-content_new.pdf |title=What's on the MCAT Exam |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref>

=== Psychological, Social and Biological Functions of Behavior ===
This section tests psychology and sociology so that students can demonstrate their understanding of the behavioral and sociocultural determinants of health. Specific material tested include behavior and behavior change, perceptions of self and others, cultural and social differences that influence well-being and social stratification. Understanding of research methods and statistics are also important to successfully reason through this material.<ref name=":0" />

=== Scientific Inquiry and Reasoning Skills ===
In the new MCAT exam, changes have been made not only in the content of the exam, but also in the way in which content is presented on the exam. MCAT questions will require examinees to demonstrate four Scientific Inquiry and Reasoning Skills that have been identified by the MR5 as crucial to success in science and medicine. The first skill is ''Knowledge of Scientific Concepts and Principles'', which requires students to not only recognize and recall scientific information, but also to identify relationships between similar concepts. ''Scientific Reasoning and Problem Solving'' tests the student's ability to relate scientific theories and formulas to presented information to explain findings and draw conclusions. ''Reasoning about the Design and Execution of Research'' requires examinees to show that they can understand science in the context of experiments. The fourth skill of ''Data-based and Statistical Reasoning'' requires students to be able to read graphs and tables and draw conclusion from evidence.<ref name=":0" />

== Scoring ==
The test consists of four sections, each scored from 118 to 132 with a median score of 125.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/applying-medical-school/article/mcat-exam-score-scale/ |title=The MCAT Exam Score Scale |access-date=2018-03-27 |language=en |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref> The total MCAT score is a sum of the scores from each of the four sections, ranging from 472 to 528 with a median score of 500. Scores are released on a pre-determined date between 30 and 35 days after the exam date.<ref>{{cite web |title=U.S. MCAT Calendar, Scheduling Deadlines, and Score Release Dates |year=2024 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/register-mcat-exam/us-mcat-calendar-scheduling-deadlines-and-score-release-dates-0}}</ref>

== Policies ==
Like some other professional exams (e.g. the [[Graduate Management Admission Test]] (GMAT) or the [[Law School Admissions Test]] (LSAT)), the MCAT may be voided on the day of the exam if the exam taker is not satisfied with his or her performance. It can be voided at any time during the exam, or during a five-minute window that begins immediately after the end of the last section. The decision to void can only be based on the test taker's self-assessment, as no scoring information is available at the time.{{cn|date=October 2023}}

The AAMC prohibits the use of calculators, timers, or other electronic devices during the MCAT exam.<ref>{{cite web |title=The MCAT Essentials for Testing Year 2016 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges |url=https://aamc-orange.global.ssl.fastly.net/production/media/filer_public/42/99/4299a220-8414-497a-8594-5b9b7d962ef1/essentials_2016_-_final_5-20-2016.pdf |year=2016}}{{rp|24−25}}</ref> Cellular phones are also strictly prohibited from testing rooms and individuals found to possess them are noted by name in a security report submitted to the AAMC. The only item that may be brought into the testing room is the candidate's photo ID. If a jacket or sweater is worn, it may not be removed in the testing room.<ref>{{cite web |title=Testing Center Regulations and Procedures |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges |url=https://www.aamc.org/students/applying/mcat/taking/85604/taking_regulations.html}}</ref>

It is no longer a rule that students must receive permission from the AAMC if they wish to take the MCAT more than three times in total. The limit with the computerized MCAT is three times per year, with a lifetime limit of seven times.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/applying-medical-school/faq/mcat-faqs/ |title=MCAT FAQ |website=students-residents.aamc.org}}</ref> An examinee can register for only one test date at a time, and must wait two days after testing before registering for a new test date.

Scaled MCAT exam results are made available to examinees approximately thirty days after the test via the AAMC's MCAT Testing History (THx) Web application. Examinees do not receive a copy of their scores in the mail, nor are examinees given their raw scores. MCAT THx is also used to transmit scores to medical schools, application services and other organizations (at no cost).

== Preparation ==
The average student spent 3 months preparing for the MCAT exam spending about 20 hours per week, excluding time taking regular courses.<ref>{{cite web |title=When Is the Right Time to Take the MCAT Exam? Three Questions to Ask Yourself |year=2024 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/taking-mcat-exam/when-right-time-take-mcat-exam-three-questions-ask-yourself}}</ref>

In the weeks leading up to the exam, most students take some time off to study intensely for the exam. The AAMC provides official study materials for purchase on their website with hundreds of questions written by the developers of the MCAT, including four scored practice exams and one non-scored practice exam.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://offers.aamc.org/mcat-study-materials-1 |title=Prepare for the MCAT Exam |website=offers.aamc.org |access-date=2018-04-16}}</ref> As of the 2023 MCAT testing cycle, 89.6% of students used official MCAT Practice Exams, while 61.2% of test-takers reported using official MCAT Question Packs and 58.5% reported using official MCAT Section Banks.<ref>{{cite report |title=Post-MCAT Questionnaire 2023 Report |year=2023 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges |url=https://www.aamc.org/media/75031/download}}</ref>

The AAMC also provides free online preparatory material for the MCAT through [[Khan Academy]], including 1,000 free videos and 2,800 review questions including content review and passage-based questions.<ref>{{cite web |title=MCAT Test prep |year=2024 |publisher=Khan Academy |url=https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat}}</ref> In 2023, 66.3% of students responded that they used this partner material to prepare for the exam.<ref>{{cite report |title=Post-MCAT Questionnaire 2023 Report |author=Association of American Medical Colleges |year=2023 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges |url=https://www.aamc.org/media/75031/download}}</ref>

== Relevance ==
[[File:Medical School Acceptance vs. MCAT 2016-2018.jpg|thumb|419x419px|Medical school acceptance based on MCAT Scores, 2016–2018<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.aamc.org/download/321508/data/factstablea23.pdf |title=MCAT and GPA Grid for Applicants and Acceptees to U.S. Medical Schools, 2016–2017 through 2017–2018 |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref>]]Almost all United States medical schools and most Canadian medical schools require prospective students to submit MCAT scores for their applications.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://students-residents.aamc.org/applying-medical-school/taking-mcat-exam/about-mcat-exam/ |title=About the MCAT® Exam |website=students-residents.aamc.org |language=en |access-date=2018-04-15}}</ref> In a survey conducted by the AAMC of 130 medical schools, MCAT scores were among the most important metrics used to identify applicants to interview and admit.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |url=https://www.aamc.org/download/462316/data/mcatguide.pdf |title=Using MCAT Data in 2018 Medical Student Selection |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref> Furthermore, in a 2017 survey by [[Kaplan, Inc.|Kaplan]], 54% of medical schools said that a low MCAT score was "the biggest application dealbreaker".<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://press.kaptest.com/press-releases/kaplan-test-prep-survey-medical-school-admissions-officers-advise-aspiring-doctors-score-high-mcat-apply-early-avoid-discussing-politics |title=Kaplan Test Prep Survey: Medical School Admissions Officers Advise Aspiring Doctors to Score High on the MCAT®, Apply Early, and Avoid Discussing Politics |date=2017-11-27 |work=Kaplan Test Prep Online Pressroom |access-date=2018-03-30 |language=en-US}}</ref> Medical school admissions is a holistic process and the AAMC provides recommendations on how MCAT scores should be used in admissions, specifically recommending that MCAT scores should not outweigh an applicant's other materials.<ref name=":3" />

A 2016 study showed a small correlation (''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.18) between MCAT scores and [[USMLE]] step 1 scores.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Giordano |first1=C. |last2=Hutchinson |first2=D. |last3=Peppler |first3=R. |year=2016 |title=A Predictive Model for United States Medical Licensing Exam (USMLE) Step 1 Scores |journal=Cureus |volume=8 |issue=9 |article-number=e769 |doi=10.7759/cureus.769 |doi-access=free |pmid=27738569 |pmc=5059149}}</ref> The MCAT exhibited a medium correlation (''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.32) with the Canadian Board exam in 2016, the ([[MCCQE]]-1).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roy |first1=B. |last2=Ripstein |first2=I. |last3=Perry |first3=K. |last4=Cohen |first4=B. |year=2016 |title=Predictive value of grade point average (GPA), Medical College Admission Test (MCAT), internal examinations (Block) and National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) scores on Medical Council of Canada qualifying examination part I (MCCQE-1) scores. |journal=Canadian Medical Education Journal |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=e47–e56 |doi=10.36834/cmej.36616 |pmid=27103953 |doi-access=free |pmc=4830373}}</ref> The Biological Sciences section had been the most directly correlated section to success on the USMLE Step 1 exam in an article published in 2002, with medium-to-large correlation coefficients of 0.55 vs 0.49 for Physical Sciences and a medium correlation of 0.40 for Verbal Reasoning.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Undergraduate Institutional MCAT Scores as Predictors of USMLE Step 1 Performance |journal=Biochemical Pharmacology |volume=24 |issue=16 |pages=1517–21 |publisher=Acad Medicine |year=2002 |pmid=8 |last1=Moroi |first1=K. |last2=Sato |first2=T. |doi=10.1097/00001888-200210001-00005}}</ref>

Results from the previous version of the MCAT that was administered between 1992 and 2014 have been studied in relation to academic success in medical school and beyond. Most data suggests that undergraduate grades and MCAT scores can predict scores on USMLE Step exams.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.aamc.org/download/462316/data/mcatguide.pdf |title=Using MCAT® Data in 2018 Medical Student Selection |publisher=Association of American Medical Colleges}}</ref> Data from a cohort of 14 medical schools in 1992 and 1993 found that MCAT scores were stronger predictors of USMLE Step scores than undergraduate GPA and were also good predictors for probability of experiencing academic difficulty.<ref name=":03">{{Cite journal |last=Julian |first=Ellen R. |s2cid=11151468 |date=October 2005 |title=Validity of the Medical College Admission Test for predicting medical school performance |journal=Academic Medicine |volume=80 |issue=10 |pages=910–917 |issn=1040-2446 |pmid=16186610 |doi=10.1097/00001888-200510000-00010 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Data from students from 119 U.S. medical schools who matriculated between 2001 and 2004 showed that undergraduate GPA and MCAT total scores predicted unimpeded progress towards medical school graduation better than GPA alone.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dunleavy |first1=Dana M. |last2=Kroopnick |first2=Marc H. |last3=Dowd |first3=Keith W. |last4=Searcy |first4=Cynthia A. |last5=Zhao |first5=Xiaohui |date=May 2013 |title=The predictive validity of the MCAT exam in relation to academic performance through medical school: a national cohort study of 2001–2004 matriculants |journal=Academic Medicine |volume=88 |issue=5 |pages=666–671 |doi=10.1097/ACM.0b013e3182864299 |issn=1938-808X |pmid=23478635 |doi-access=free}}</ref> A third study using data from students from the [[University of Minnesota Medical School]] from five graduating classes between 2011 and 2015, found that MCAT component scores were significantly associated with USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 scores, although the effect was small.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gauer |first1=Jacqueline L. |last2=Wolff |first2=Josephine M. |last3=Jackson |first3=J. Brooks |date=2016-09-30 |title=Do MCAT scores predict USMLE scores? An analysis on 5 years of medical student data |journal=Medical Education Online |volume=21 |article-number=31795 |doi=10.3402/meo.v21.31795 |pmc=5045966 |pmid=27702431}}</ref> Higher MCAT scores are correlated with membership in the national medical honors society [[Alpha Omega Alpha]], suggesting that MCAT scores can be useful to identify potential top-performing medical students.<ref>{{Cite journal |pmc=5608086 |title=Association between the Medical College Admission Test scores and Alpha Omega Alpha Medical Honors Society membership |journal=Advances in Medical Education and Practice |volume=8 |pages=627–632 |year=2017 |last1=Gauer |first1=J. L. |last2=Jackson |first2=J. B. |pmid=28979178 |doi=10.2147/AMEP.S145839 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Since the most recent version of the MCAT exam was only released in 2015, insufficient years have passed to determine correlation between MCAT scores and medical school benchmarks. The AAMC plans to use medical school data from 2017 to 2021 to determine the predictive ability of the new MCAT.<ref name=":3" /> The data will be collected from 18 medical schools who have agreed to collect data from students from entry to graduation including academic performance, USMLE Step exam scores, time to graduation and graduation rates.<ref name=":03" />

======================================================================
ARTICLE: Memory span
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{Short description|Longest list of items one can memorize immediately}}
In [[psychology]] and [[neuroscience]], '''memory span''' is the longest list of items that a person can repeat back in correct order immediately after presentation on 50% of all trials. Items may include [[Word|words]], [[Number|numbers]], or [[Letter (alphabet)|letters]]. The task is known as ''digit span'' when numbers are used. Memory span is a common measure of [[working memory]] and [[short-term memory]]. It is also a component of cognitive ability tests such as the [[Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale]] (WAIS). Backward memory span is a more challenging variation which involves recalling items in reverse order.

==As a functional aspect==
Functionally, memory span is used to measure the number of discrete units over which the individual can successively distribute their attention and still organize them into a working unit. To generalize, it refers to the ability of an individual to reproduce immediately, after one presentation, a series of discrete stimuli in their original order.<ref>Albert B. Blankenship(1938). The psychological bulletin, Vol. 35, No. 1, 2-3.</ref> Therefore memory span can be understood as the quantum of action of thought.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Weiss | first1=Volkmar | title=Memory span as the quantum of action of thought | journal=Cahiers de Psychologie Cognitive | date=January 1995 | volume=14 | pages=387–408 | url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/288034156 }}</ref>

Experiments in memory span have found that the more familiar a person is with the type of subject matter presented to them, the more they will remember it in a novel setting. For example, a person will better remember a sequence in their first-language than their second-language; a person will also remember a sequence of words better than they would a sequence of nonsense syllables.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Jones|first1=Gary|last2=Macken|first2=Bill|date=2015|title=Questioning short-term memory and its measurement: Why digit span measures long-term associative learning|journal=Cognition|volume=144|doi=10.1016/j.cognition.2015.07.009|pmid=26209910|pages=1–13|doi-access=free}}</ref>

According to a theory by [[Alan Baddeley]] and [[Graham Hitch]], working memory is under the influence of [[Baddeley's model of working memory|three key mechanisms]]: the visuospatial sketchpad, the central executive, and the phonological loop. A mechanism called the episodic buffer was later added to the model. The phonological loop is the mechanism that facilitates learning and memory by storing information (in the articulatory loop) and refreshing or rehearsing it in memory (in the acoustic store).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Karatekin|first=Canan|date=2004|title=A test of the integrity of the components of Baddeley's model of working memory in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)|journal=Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry|volume=45|issue=5|pages=912–926|doi=10.1111/j.1469-7610.2004.t01-1-00285.x|pmid=15225335}}</ref> The phonological similarity effect is when items in a list have similar features (e.g. similar sound), they are more difficult to remember. Likewise, the more different the items in a list are, the easier it is to recall them.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chow|first1=Michael|last2=Macnamara|first2=Brooke N.|last3=Conway|first3=Andrew R. A.|date=April 2016|title=Phonological similarity in working memory span tasks|journal=Memory & Cognition|volume=44|issue=6|doi=10.3758/s13421-016-0609-8|pmid=27048510|pages=937–949|doi-access=free}}</ref> Memory span tasks since the formulation of Baddeley and Hitch's theory have been helpful as support for the phonological loop as part of the working memory.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baddeley|first1=Alan|last2=Gathercole|first2=Susan|last3=Papagno|first3=Costanza|title=The phonological loop as a language learning device.|journal=Psychological Review|volume=105|issue=1|pages=158–173|doi=10.1037/0033-295x.105.1.158|pmid=9450375|date=January 1998|citeseerx=10.1.1.464.9511|s2cid=15650449 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Baddeley|first=A. D.|date=1966-11-01|title=Short-term memory for word sequences as a function of acoustic, semantic and formal similarity|journal=Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology|volume=18|issue=4|pages=362–365|doi=10.1080/14640746608400055|issn=0033-555X|pmid=5956080|s2cid=32498516|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==As a structural aspect==
A structural definition of memory span is difficult to give, for one immediately is faced by the distinctions between the prerequisites for memory span, and the actual processes involved. "Associability” is required in memory span. This term refers to the ability of the subject to group the series of elements together: to perceive relationships among the series in order to better reproduce them. Still, another process involved in memory span is that of imagery. The subject, in order to be able to reproduce the series presented, must be able to image the series. The actual reproducing of the series of stimuli involves the process of memory. If the individual possessed no memory at all, reproduction of the series would be impossible.  It is also known that memory span and memory are different in the length of time over which reproduction is possible. Memory span is transitory; memory is fairly permanent. In addition, the amount of material involved in memory span is ordinarily much less than the amount of material involved in memory. Reproduction of the series also involves certain other "reproduction factors," such as language ability and arithmetical proficiency.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Humstone | first1 = H. J. | year = 1919 | title = Memory Span Tests | journal = Psychol. Clin. | volume = 12 | issue = 5–9| pages = 196–200 | pmid = 28909279 | pmc = 5076260 }}</ref>

==Digit-span==
A digit-span task is used to measure [[working memory]]'s number storage capacity. Participants see or hear a sequence of numerical digits and are tasked to recall the sequence correctly, with increasingly longer sequences being tested in each trial. The participant's span is the longest number of sequential digits that can accurately be remembered. Digit-span tasks can be given forwards or backwards, meaning that once the sequence is presented, the participant is asked to either recall the sequence in normal or reverse order.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.neurobs.com/ex_files/expt_view?id=218 | title=Neurobehavioral Systems}}</ref> Digit-span tasks are the most commonly used test for memory span, partially because performance on a digit-span task cannot be affected by factors such as semantics, frequency of appearance in daily life, complexity, etc.<ref name=":0" />{{Infobox diagnostic |
|Name=Memory span|Image=Sample-digit-span-test-results.gif|Caption=This is a graphical representation of typical results that might be obtained from performing a forward/backward digit span recall task on participants in several different age groups.  The numbers on the y-axis indicate number of digits successfully recalled.|ICD10=|ICD9=|MeshID=D011581|OPS301=|OtherCodes=}}

<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Sample-average-results.gif|thumb|WAIS-III and WMS-III Variables Mean Scores.]] -->Verbal working memory is involved in many everyday tasks, such as remembering a friend's telephone number while entering it into a phone and understanding long and difficult sentences.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Schwering SC, MacDonald MC | title = Verbal Working Memory as Emergent from Language Comprehension and Production | journal = Frontiers in Human Neuroscience | date=12 March 2020 | volume = 14 | article-number = 68 | doi=10.3389/fnhum.2020.00068 | pmid = 32226368 | pmc = 7081770 | doi-access = free }}</ref>{{citation needed|date=October 2014}} Verbal working memory is also thought to be one of the elements underlying intelligence (often referred to as ''IQ'', meaning '[[intelligence quotient]]'); thus, the digit span task is a common component of many IQ tests, including the widely used [[Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale]] (WAIS). Performance on the digit span task is also closely linked to language learning abilities; improving [[verbal memory]] capacities may therefore aid mastery of a new language.<ref>Cambridge Brain Science. About this test: Improve your digit-span performance by 'chunking'. Medical Research Council. http://www.cambridgebrainsciences.com/browse/memory/test/digit-span</ref><ref>Sage Journals. Reliable Digit Span A Systematic Review and Cross-Validation Study. Ryan W. Schroeder, Philip Twumasi-Ankrah, Lyle E. Baade and Paul S. Marshall. 6 December 2011. http://asm.sagepub.com/content/19/1/21.abstract</ref><ref>Sage Journals. WAIS Digit Span-Based Indicators of Malingered Neurocognitive Dysfunction Classification Accuracy in Traumatic Brain Injury. Matthew T. Heinly, Kevin W. Greve, Kevin J. Bianchini, Jeffery M. Love and Adrianne Brennan. http://asm.sagepub.com/content/12/4/429.short</ref>

==Factors==
There are a number of factors which affect memory span. Some of the factors are extrinsic, or present in the testing situation itself. These factors, if not carefully controlled, cause the memory span test to be statistically unreliable. While the existence of many of these factors have been recognized, extensive studies on their importance have yet to be done. Some of these extrinsic factors include stimulus grouping, response grouping, presentation rate, and S-R compatibility.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Buffardi|first=Louis|date=1972-01-01|title=Factors Affecting Memory Span in Binary and Octal Responding|jstor=1420838|journal=The American Journal of Psychology|volume=85|issue=3|pages=377–391|doi=10.2307/1420838}}</ref>

Other factors are intrinsic in the individual, and it is these factors which are the basis of "true" memory span. Though numerous factors affect memory span, the test is one that shows surprisingly high reliability. Results obtained by different investigators show that the reliability coefficients for memory span are quite high. {{citation needed|date=August 2016}}

===Extrinsic factors===
# Characteristics of materials used: If the material is all closely related, it will be more easily reproduced than if it is unrelated. This relationship of the material is called the "coefficient of associability."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hockey|first=Robert|date=1973-02-01|title=Rate of presentation in running memory and direct manipulation of input-processing strategies|journal=Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology|volume=25|issue=1|pages=104–111|doi=10.1080/14640747308400328|s2cid=144647200|issn=0033-555X}}</ref> For example, in spoken word-span tasks if the words presented are phonologically similar a lower span is elicited than if the task uses phonologically different words.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Cecchetto|first1=Carlo|last2=Giustolisi|first2=Beatrice|last3=Mantovan|first3=Lara|date=2016-09-01|title=Short-term memory and sign languages: sign span and its linguistic implications|url=https://doaj.org/article/8a80d2a902ca4205b8286ccb8ca540a2|journal=Linguística: Revista de Estudos Linguísticos da Universidade do Porto|language=en|volume=11|issue=a11|issn=1646-6195}}</ref>
# Addition of non-target elements: the addition of irrelevant stimuli between target stimuli reduces performance on memory span tasks. If the irrelevant stimuli is a repeated syllable (i.e. ''ba'', ''ba'', ''ba'') the span is reduced ([[articulatory suppression]] effect).<ref name=":1" />
# Rhythm of presentation: Closely related to the problem of presenting the stimuli in groups, is the presentation of the stimuli in rhythmic fashion. Most investigators point out that the stimuli used in testing memory span should be presented with as little rhythm as possible. The effect of rhythm is to group the units in the series, again enabling the individual to secure a span higher than their "true" one. {{citation needed|date=March 2021}}
# Rate of presentation: The speed with which the stimuli are presented has an effect on memory span score. When listening to auditory stimuli, the impact of speed is mediated by whether the subject is actively or passively listening. Active listeners score better with faster stimuli presentation. Passive listeners score better as time increases.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Drewnowski|first1=Adam|last2=Murdock|first2=Bennet B.|date=1980-05-01|title=The role of auditory features in memory span for words.|url=http://content.apa.org/journals/xlm/6/3/319|journal=Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning & Memory|language=en|volume=6|issue=3|pages=319–332|doi=10.1037/0278-7393.6.3.319|pmid=7373250|issn=0096-1515|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
# Modality of presentation: Studies have shown a consistent increase in memory span for lists presented auditorally over ones presented visually.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Drewnowski|first=A.|author2=Murdock, B. B.|title=The role of auditory features in memory span for words|journal=Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory|year=1980|volume=6|issue=3|pages=319–332|doi=10.1037/0278-7393.6.3.319|pmid=7373250}}</ref> This can be seen in performance on memory span tasks for signed languages, which typically yield lower spans than spoken languages.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Boutla|first1=Mrim|last2=Supalla|first2=Ted|last3=Newport|first3=Elissa L|last4=Bavelier|first4=Daphne|title=Short-term memory span: insights from sign language|journal=Nature Neuroscience|volume=7|issue=9|pages=997–1002|doi=10.1038/nn1298|pmc=2945821|pmid=15311279|year=2004}}</ref>
# Time required to vocalize responses: Memory span is approximately equal to the number of items which an individual can articulate in two seconds.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ellis | first1 = N. C. | last2 = Hennelly | first2 = R. A. | year = 1980 | title = A bilingual word-length effect: Implications for intelligence testing and the relative ease of mental calculation in Welsh and English | journal = British Journal of Psychology | volume = 71 | issue = 1| pages = 43–51 | doi = 10.1111/j.2044-8295.1980.tb02728.x }}</ref> With that in mind, memory span is consistently higher for short words than for long words.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Baddeley | first1 = A. D. | last2 = Thomson | first2 = N. | last3 = Buchanan | first3 = M. | year = 1975 | title = Word length and the structure of short-term memory | journal = Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior | volume = 14 | issue = 6| pages = 575–589 | doi = 10.1016/S0022-5371(75)80045-4 }}</ref> This factor helps account for cross-linguistic differences on digit memory span tasks.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chan|first1=MeowLan E|last2=Elliott|first2=John M|date=2011-03-01|title=Cross-Linguistic Differences in Digit Memory Span|journal=Australian Psychologist|language=en|volume=46|issue=1|pages=25–30|doi=10.1111/j.1742-9544.2010.00007.x|s2cid=142535888|issn=1742-9544}}</ref>
# Method of scoring responses: The method of scoring responses also has an effect upon the perceived memory span of the individual. Variations in scoring are common and should be considered when looking at data.
# Distraction: Interference negatively effects performance on memory span tasks. Since distraction is harder to ignore at a young age, it is possible that interference may have a role in the differences of scores based on age.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lustig | first1 = C. | last2 = May | first2 = C. P. | last3 = Hasher | first3 = L. | year = 2001 | title = Working memory span and the role of proactive interference | journal = Journal of Experimental Psychology | volume = 130 | issue = 2| pages = 199–207 | doi=10.1037/0096-3445.130.2.199| pmid = 11409099 }}</ref>

===Intrinsic factors===
There are certain intrinsic factors specific to each individual that may affect the extent, or span, of one's working memory.

;Age

An individual's age affects their working memory span. During [[Child|childhood]] and adolescent development, memory span improves with age. After [[Adult|adulthood]] is reached, memory span slowly decreases as an individual progresses towards old age. The decline in memory span with old age has been associated with a decrease of working memory storage and processing, and the [[Memory and aging|age difference in working memory]] becomes greater as the memory tasks performed become more difficult.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Schroeder|first=Paul J|date=May 2014|title=The effects of age on processing and storage in working memory span tasks and reading comprehension.|journal=Experimental Aging Research|volume=40|issue=3|pages=308–31|doi=10.1080/0361073X.2014.896666|pmid=24785593|s2cid=23928682}}</ref> Generally, the decline in working memory and memory span tasks in old age is attributed to a decline in overall [[Executive functions|cognitive control]]. One of the key aspects of working memory is the ability to inhibit distractions and to focus on stimulus cues. As a person ages, these abilities diminish, which reduces effective memory.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hills|first1=Thomas T.|last2=Mata|first2=Rui|last3=Wilke|first3=Andreas|last4=Samanez-Larkin|first4=Gregory R|date=December 1, 2014|title=Mechanisms of Age-Related Decline in Memory Search Across the Adult Life Span|journal=Developmental Psychology|volume=49|issue=12|doi=10.1037/a0032272|pmid=23586941|pmc=3842414|pages=2396–404}}</ref>

;Practice of music

[[Music education|Musical training]] improves the verbal memory span, but there is no consensus among researchers if it improves visual working memory capacity. The more training received the better the [[memory improvement]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ho | first1 = Y. C. | last2 = Cheung | first2 = M.C. | last3 = Chan | first3 = A.S. | year = 2003 | title = Music training improves verbal but not visual memory: Cross-sectional and longitudinal explorations in children | journal = Neuropsychology | volume = 17 | issue = 3| pages = 439–450 | doi=10.1037/0894-4105.17.3.439 | pmid=12959510| citeseerx = 10.1.1.582.7292 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Chan | first1 = A. S. | last2 = Ho | first2 = Y. | last3 = Cheung | first3 = M. | year = 1998 | title = Music training improves verbal memory | journal = Nature | volume = 396 | issue = 6707| page = 128 | doi = 10.1038/24075 | pmid = 9823892 | bibcode = 1998Natur.396..128C | s2cid = 4425221 | doi-access = free }}</ref>  Preschoolers given short-term musical training showed improvement in their executive function and verbal memory span.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Moreno | first1 = S. | last2 = Bialystok | first2 = E. | last3 = Barac | first3 = R. | last4 = Schellenberg | first4 = E.G. | last5 = Cepeda | first5 = N.J. | last6 = Chau | first6 = T. | year = 2011 | title = Short-term music training enhances verbal intelligence and executive function | journal = Psychological Science | volume = 22 | issue = 11| pages = 1425–1433 | doi = 10.1177/0956797611416999 | pmid=21969312 | pmc=3449320}}</ref>  Sixty to eighty-five year-olds who received [[piano]] lessons showed a decrease of age-based memory decline, as well as improved executive function and working memory.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Bugos | first1 = J. A. | last2 = Perlstein | first2 = W. M. | last3 = McCrae | first3 = C. S. | last4 = Brophy | first4 = T. S. | last5 = Bedenbaugh | first5 = P. H. | year = 2007 | title = Individualized Piano Instruction enhances executive functioning and working memory in older adults | journal = Aging & Mental Health | volume = 11 | issue = 4| pages = 464–471 | doi = 10.1080/13607860601086504 | pmid = 17612811 | s2cid = 3454284 }}</ref>  Musicians also perform significantly better on the rhythm span test (the results of which correlate significantly with results of the digit span test).<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Schaal | first1 = Nora K. | last2 = Banissy | first2 = Michael J. | last3 = Lange | first3 = Kathrin | year = 2015 | title = The Rhythm Span Task: Comparing Memory Capacity for Musical Rhythms in Musicians and Non-Musicians | url = http://research.gold.ac.uk/10607/1/PSY-Banissy-2014.pdf| journal = Journal of New Music Research | volume = 44 | issue = 1| pages = 3–10 | doi = 10.1080/09298215.2014.937724 | s2cid = 14363658 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Saito | first1 = Satoru | year = 2001 | title =  The phonological loop and memory for rhythms: an individual differences approach| journal = Memory | volume = 9 | issue = 4–6| pages = 313–322 | doi = 10.1080/09658210143000164 | pmid = 11594354 | s2cid = 31923026 }}</ref> Musicians perform better on verbal tone-based memory span tasks than non-musicians; however they do not perform better than non-musicians if the tones in a verbal task are across multiple words.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yu|first1=Lijun|last2=Li|first2=Xiaonuo|last3=Yu|first3=Hua|last4=Cui|first4=Zhuoya|last5=Liao|first5=Wenchen|last6=Li|first6=Sha|last7=Peng|first7=Yu|last8=Wang|first8=Zhaoxin|date=2016-09-01|title=Musicians have larger memory spans for Mandarin tones but not segments|journal=Psychology of Music|language=en|volume=44|issue=5|pages=1058–1067|doi=10.1177/0305735615608695|s2cid=148174452|issn=0305-7356}}</ref>

==The memory span procedure==
In a typical test of memory span, a list of random numbers or letters is read out loud or presented on a computer screen at the rate of one per second. The test begins with two to three numbers, increasing until the person commits errors. Recognizable patterns (for example 2, 4, 6, 8) should be avoided. At the end of a sequence, the person being tested is asked to recall the items in order. The average digit span for normal adults without error is [[seven plus or minus two]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Miller | first1 = G. | author-link = George Armitage Miller | year = 1956 | title = The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two–The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information | journal = Psychological Review | volume = 63 | issue = 2| pages = 81–97 | doi=10.1037/h0043158 | pmid=13310704| title-link = The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two–The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information | citeseerx = 10.1.1.308.8071 | s2cid = 15654531 }}</ref> However, memory span can be expanded dramatically – in one case to 80 digits – by learning a sophisticated [[mnemonic]] system of recoding rules by which substrings of 5 to 10 digits are translated into one new chunk.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ericsson | first1 = K. A. | last2 = Delaney | first2 = P. F. | last3 = Weaver | first3 = G. | last4 = Mahadevan | first4 = R. | year = 2004 | title = Uncovering the structure of a memorist's superior "basic" memory capacity | journal = Cognitive Psychology | volume = 49 | issue = 3| pages = 191–237 | doi=10.1016/j.cogpsych.2004.02.001| pmid = 15342260 | s2cid = 14121645 }}</ref> In December 2019, Ryu Song I entered the ''[[Guinness World Records|Guinness Book of World Records]]'' for memorizing a sequence of 547 digits spoken aloud at the rate of one per second at the [[World Memory Championships|World Memory Championship]] in Wuhan, China.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Most spoken numbers memorized at a rate of 1 per second |newspaper=Guinness World Records |url=https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/360576-most-spoken-numbers-memorised-at-rate-of-1-per-second}}</ref>

In a backward digit span task, the procedure is largely the same, except that subjects being tested are asked to recall the digits in backward order (e.g., if presented with the following string of numbers "1 5 9 2 3," the subject would be asked to recall the digits in reverse order; in the case, the correct response would be "3 2 9 5 1").

Other memory span tests focus on both a processing task and a memory storage task. Generally, the task involves alternating between a task that requires mental processing and cognition, and a word or digit that needs to be memorized. For example, the processing question might involve the participant checking if an arithmetic problem is correct, or reading a sentence and answering a comprehension question about its meaning. The participant would then be presented with a word to memorize, before moving on to the next processing question. When the exercise is complete, the participant will try to recall as many words as possible. When Daneman and Carpenter investigated this method in 1980, they found a strong correlation between the number of words memorized and the comprehension performance for the processing questions. In other words, those who had a high memory span score and could recall many of the words also performed well on the processing questions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://revel.pearson.com/#/courses/579b8212e4b0b1bce3727cce/player?pageId=a9e05cfadf556d7d312437b5af6498c546d3a8770-e40cc85d69c345b08c596d531a9501b3&assignmentId=ced9193a-95f1-46fe-ba59-e5e7c95bb871|title=Cognition|last1=Radvansky|first1=Gabriel|last2=Ashcraft|first2=Mark|date=2016|website=Pearson|publisher=Pearson Education Inc.|access-date=3 September 2016}}</ref>

==From simple span to complex span==
Research in the 1970s has shown that memory span with digits and words is only weakly related to performance in complex cognitive tasks such as text comprehension, which are assumed to depend on short-term memory.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Perfetti | first1 = C. A. | last2 = Goldman | first2 = S. R. | year = 1976 | title = Discourse memory and reading comprehension skill | journal = Journal of Verbal Learning & Verbal Behavior | volume = 15 | pages = 33–42 | doi=10.1016/s0022-5371(76)90004-9}}</ref> This questioned the interpretation of memory span as a measure of the capacity of a central [[short-term memory]] or [[working memory]]. Daneman and Carpenter introduced an extended version of the memory span task which they called [[reading span]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Daneman | first1 = M. | last2 = Carpenter | first2 = P. A. | year = 1980 | title = Individual differences in working memory and reading | journal = Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior | volume = 19 | issue = 4| pages = 450–466 | doi=10.1016/s0022-5371(80)90312-6| s2cid = 144899071 }}</ref>

The reading span task was the first instance of the family of ''complex span'' tasks, which differ from the traditional ''simple span'' tasks by adding a processing demand to the requirement to remember a list of items. In complex span tasks encoding of the memory items (e.g., words) alternates with brief processing episodes (e.g., reading sentences). For example, the operation span task combines verification of brief mathematical equations such as "2+6/2 = 5?" with memory for a word or a letter that follows immediately after each equation.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Turner | first1 = M. L. | last2 = Engle | first2 = R. W. | year = 1989 | title = Is working memory capacity task dependent? | journal = Journal of Memory and Language | volume = 28 | issue = 2| pages = 127–154 | doi=10.1016/0749-596x(89)90040-5}}</ref> Complex-span tasks have also been shown to be closely related to many other aspects of complex cognitive performance besides language comprehension, among other things to measures of fluid intelligence.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Kane | first1 = M. J. | last2 = Hambrick | first2 = D. Z. | last3 = Tuholski | first3 = S. W. | last4 = Wilhelm | first4 = O. | last5 = Payne | first5 = T. W. | last6 = Engle | first6 = R. W. | year = 2004 | title = The generality of working-memory capacity: A latent-variable approach to verbal and visuo-spatial memory span and reasoning | journal = Journal of Experimental Psychology: General | volume = 133 | issue = 2| pages = 189–217 | doi=10.1037/0096-3445.133.2.189| pmid = 15149250 | citeseerx = 10.1.1.517.3056 | s2cid = 266965 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Conway | first1 = A. R. A. | last2 = Kane | first2 = M. J. | last3 = Bunting | first3 = M. F. | last4 = Hambrick | first4 = D. Z. | last5 = Wilhelm | first5 = O. | last6 = Engle | first6 = R. W. | year = 2005 | title = Working memory span tasks: A methodological review and user's guide | journal = Psychonomic Bulletin & Review | volume = 12 | issue = 5| pages = 769–786 | doi=10.3758/bf03196772| pmid = 16523997 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==The role of interference==
There is the possibility that susceptibility to [[proactive interference]] (PI) affects performance on memory span measures. For older adults, span estimates increased with each PI-reducing manipulation; for younger adults, scores increased when multiple PI manipulations were combined or when PI-reducing manipulations were used in paradigms in which within-task PI was especially high. It is suggested that PI critically influences span performance. There might be the possibility that interference-proneness may influence cognitive behaviors previously thought to be governed by capacity.

PI-reducing procedures did act to improve span scores in many instances. The impact of PI is greater for older adults than for younger adults. Older adults showed relatively poor span performance when PI was maximal. By contrast, younger adults improved only when PI reductions were combined, suggesting that they are relatively resistant to PI. The fact that PI contributes to span performance raises a number of interesting possibilities with respect to previously held assumptions based on memory span performance. Working memory span tasks may measure interference-proneness in addition to capacity for both older and younger adults, suggest that resistance to interference may also affect performance on many cognitive tasks. Indeed, other studies show that individual differences in susceptibility to PI are predictive of scores on standard achievement tests.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = May | first1 = C.P. | last2 = Hasher | first2 = L. | last3 = Kane | first3 = M.J. | year = 1999 | title = The role of interference in memory span | journal = Memory & Cognition | volume = 27 | issue = 5| pages = 759–767 | doi=10.3758/bf03198529 | pmid=10540805| doi-access = free }}</ref>

ARTICLE: Metacognition
