======================================================================
ARTICLE: Test anxiety
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{Short description|Anxiety or stress triggered by exams}}
'''Test anxiety''' is a combination of physiological over-arousal, [[Stress (biology)|tension]] and somatic symptoms, along with [[Worry|worry, dread]], [[fear of failure]], and [[Exaggeration|catastrophizing]], that occur before or during test situations.<ref name= "Zeidner">Zeidner M. (1998). ''Test anxiety: The state of the art''. New York, NY: Plenum</ref> It is a psychological condition in which people experience extreme stress, [[anxiety]], and discomfort during and/or before taking a [[Exam|test]]. This anxiety creates significant barriers to learning and performance.<ref name = "Andrews & Wilding, 2004" >{{cite journal | last1 = Andrews | first1 = B. | last2 = Wilding | first2 = J. M. | year = 2004 | title = The relation of depression and anxiety to life-stress and achievement in students | journal = British Journal of Psychology | volume = 95 | issue = 4| pages = 509–521 | doi=10.1348/0007126042369802| pmid = 15527535 }}</ref> Research suggests that high levels of emotional distress have a direct correlation to reduced academic performance and higher overall student drop-out rates.<ref name="Andrews & Wilding, 2004"/><ref name = "Pritchard & Wilson, 2003">{{cite journal | last1 = Pritchard | first1 = M. E. | last2 = Wilson | first2 = G. S. | year = 2003 | title = Using emotional and social factors to predict student success | journal = Journal of College Student Development | volume = 44 | pages = 18–28 | doi=10.1353/csd.2003.0008| s2cid = 16769612 }}</ref><ref name = "Vaez & Laflamme, 2008">{{cite journal | last1 = Vaez | first1 = M. | last2 = Laflamme | first2 = L. | year = 2008 | title = Experienced stress, psychological symptoms, self-rated health and academic achievement: A longitudinal study of Swedish university students | journal = Social Behavior and Personality | volume = 36 | issue = 2| pages = 183–196 | doi=10.2224/sbp.2008.36.2.183| doi-access = free }}</ref> Test anxiety can have broader consequences, negatively affecting a student's social, emotional and behavioural development, as well as their feelings about themselves and school.<ref name="Salend">{{cite journal | last1 = Salend | first1 = S. J. | year = 2012 | title = Teaching students not to sweat the test | journal = Phi Delta Kappan | volume = 93 | issue = 6| pages = 20–25 | doi=10.1177/003172171209300605| s2cid = 144098336 }}</ref>

Highly test-anxious students score about 12 percentile points below their low anxiety peers.<ref name= "Hembree">{{cite journal | last1 = Hembree | first1 = R | year = 1988 | title = Correlates, Causes, Effects and Treatment of Test Anxiety | journal = Review of Educational Research | volume = 58 | issue = 1| pages = 47–77 | doi=10.3102/00346543058001047| s2cid = 27947882 }}</ref><ref name= "Cassady & Johnson">Cassidy, J & Johnson. R. (2001). Cognitive Test Anxiety and Academic Performance. [[Contemporary Educational Psychology]], 27, 270-295</ref><ref name= "McDonald">{{cite journal | last1 = McDonald | first1 = A | year = 2001 | title = The Prevalence and Effects of Test Anxiety in School Children | journal = Educational Psychology | volume = 21 | issue = 1| pages = 89–101 | doi=10.1080/01443410020019867| s2cid = 144222364 }}</ref>  Test anxiety is prevalent amongst the student populations of the world.<ref name = "Lowe & Ang, 2012">{{cite journal | last1 = Lowe | first1 = P. A. | last2 = Ang | first2 = R. P. | year = 2012 | title = Cross-cultural examination of test anxiety among US and Singapore students on the Test Anxiety Scale for Elementary Students (TAS-E) | journal = Educational Psychology | volume = 32 | issue = 1| pages = 107–126 | doi=10.1080/01443410.2011.625625| s2cid = 146529864 }}</ref><ref name="Dalkiran, Baltaci, Karatas & Nacakci, 2014">{{cite journal |last1=Dalkiran |first1=E. |last2=Baltaci |first2=H. Ş. |last3=Karatas |first3=Z. |last4=Nacakci |first4=Z. |year=2014 |title=Developing of individual instrument performance anxiety scale: Validity-reliability study |journal=International Journal of Assessment Tools in Education |volume=1 |issue=22374 |pages=13–25 |doi=10.21449/ijate.239569 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It has been studied formally since the early 1950s beginning with researchers George Mandler and Seymour Sarason.<ref>The original research and development of the TAQ (Test Anxiety Questionnaire) was conducted by: {{cite journal | last1 = Mandler | first1 = G. | last2 = Sarason | first2 = S. B. | year = 1952 | title = A study of anxiety and learning | journal = Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology | volume = 47 | issue = 2| pages = 166–173 | doi=10.1037/h0062855| pmid = 14937950 }}</ref> Sarason's brother, Irwin G. Sarason, then contributed to early investigation of test anxiety, clarifying the relationship between the focused effects of test anxiety, other focused forms of anxiety, and generalized anxiety.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Sarason | first1 = I.G. | year = 1960 | title = Empirical findings and theoretical problems in the use of anxiety scales | journal = Psychological Bulletin | volume = 57 | issue = 5| pages = 403–415 | doi=10.1037/h0041113| pmid = 13746471 }}</ref>

Test anxiety can also be labeled as [[anticipatory anxiety]], situational anxiety or evaluation anxiety. Some anxiety is normal and often helpful to stay mentally and physically alert.<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://brain.edusoft.ro/index.php/brain/article/view/131/260 | title=The Impact of Test Anxiety on Test Performance among Iranian EFL Learners |author1=Parviz Birjandi  |author2=Minoo Alemi  |name-list-style=amp | journal=BRAIN. Broad Research in Artificial Intelligence and Neuroscience |date=October 2010 | volume=1 | issue=4 | pages=45}}</ref> When one experiences too much anxiety, however, it can result in emotional or physical distress, difficulty concentrating, and emotional worry. Inferior performance arises not because of intellectual problems or poor academic preparation, but because testing situations create a sense of threat for those experiencing test anxiety; anxiety resulting from the sense of threat then disrupts attention and memory function.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Sarason | first1 = I.G. | year = 1957 | title = Test anxiety, general anxiety, and intellectual performance | journal = Journal of Consulting Psychology | volume = 21 | issue = 6| pages = 485–490 | doi=10.1037/h0043012| pmid = 13481208 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Sarason | first1 = I.G. | year = 1959 | title = Intellectual and personality correlates of test anxiety | journal = The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology | volume = 59 | issue = 2| pages = 272–275 | doi=10.1037/h0042200| pmid = 14441705 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Sarason | first1 = I.G. | year = 1963 | title = Test anxiety and intellectual performance | journal = The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology | volume = 66 | pages = 73–75 | doi=10.1037/h0047059| pmid = 13991467 }}</ref><ref>Sarason, I.G. Sarason, B.G. Pierce, G.R. (1995). Cognitive interference: At the intelligence–personality crossroads. In D.H. Saklofske & M. Zeidner, (Eds.) ''International handbook of personality and intelligence'' (pp. 285-296).  New York: Plenum Press.</ref> Researchers suggest that between 25 and 40 percent of students experience test anxiety.<ref>Cassady, J.C. (2010). Test anxiety: Contemporary theories and implications for learning. In J.C. Cassady (Ed.), ''Anxiety in schools: The causes, consequences, and solutions for academic anxieties'' (pp. 7-26). New York, NY: Peter Lang,</ref> Students with disabilities and students in gifted educations classes tend to experience high rates of test anxiety.<ref name = "Nelson & Harwood, 2011">{{cite journal | last1 = Nelson | first1 = J.M. | last2 = Harwood | first2 = H. | year = 2011 | title = Learning disabilities and anxiety: A meta-analysis | journal = Journal of Learning Disabilities | volume = 44 | issue = 1| pages = 3–17 | doi=10.1177/0022219409359939| pmid = 20375288 | s2cid = 25623149 }}</ref> Students who experience test anxiety tend to be easily distracted during a test, experience difficulty with comprehending relatively simple instructions, and have trouble organizing or recalling relevant information.<ref name="Zeidner"/>

==Signs and symptoms==

[[File:V.M. Doroshevich-East and War-Student of University of Madras.png|thumb|right|A student of the [[University of Madras]], with his hair tied to a nail in the wall, to prevent him from falling asleep (1905)]]

Researchers believe that feelings of anxiety arise to prepare a person for threats.<ref name="DePhil">DePhil, M.B., Brilot, B., Nettle, D. (2011). Anxiety: An Evolutionary Approach. Canadian Journal of Psychiatry, 56(12):707-715</ref> In humans, anxiety symptoms are distributed along a continuum and different symptom levels of anxiety predict outcomes. Responses consist of increased heart rate, [[stress hormone]] secretion, restlessness, vigilance, and fear of a potentially dangerous environment.<ref name="DePhil"/> Anxiety prepares the body physically, cognitively, and behaviourally to detect and deal with threats to survival. As a result, a person's body begins to hyperventilate to allow more oxygen to enter the bloodstream, divert blood to muscles, and sweat to cool the skin.<ref name="DePhil"/> In  individuals, the degree to which an anxiety response is developed is based on the probability of bad things happening in the environment and the individual's ability to cope with them. In the case of test taking, this might be a failing exam grade that prevents the student from being accepted to a post-secondary institution. A person's beliefs about their own competencies are a form of self-knowledge, which plays an important role in analyzing situations that might be threatening. When a person has feelings of low competence about their abilities they are likely to anticipate negative outcomes such as failure, under uncertain conditions. Thus, evaluative situations including tests and exams, are perceived as more threatening by students who have low competencies.<ref name="Putwain"/>

There is a difference between [[generalized anxiety disorder]]s (GAD) and test anxiety. GAD is characterized by "trait anxiety" which results in a person experiencing high levels of stress across a wide range of situations. In contrast, people with test anxiety have a "state anxiety" which results in high levels of nervousness specific to testing.<ref>sady, J.C. (2010). Test anxiety: Contemporary theories and implications for learning. In J.C. Cassady (Ed.), Anxiety in schools: The causes, consequences, and solutions for academic anxieties (pp. 7-26). New York, NY: Peter Lang</ref>

Symptoms of test anxiety can range from moderate to severe. "Students who exhibit moderate symptoms are still able to perform relatively well on exams. Other students with severe anxiety will often experience [[panic attacks]]."<ref>{{cite web|last=Cherry|first=Kendra|title=Test Anxiety Symptoms|url=http://psychology.about.com/od/mentalhealth/a/test-anxiety-symptoms.htm|work=The New York Times Company|accessdate=26 April 2012|archive-date=1 December 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111201181000/http://psychology.about.com/od/mentalhealth/a/test-anxiety-symptoms.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Bad physical symptoms include: headache, upset stomach, feeling of fear, feeling of dread, [[shortness of breath]], sweating, pacing or fidgeting, crying, [[racing thoughts]] and blanking out.

During states of excitement or stress, the body releases [[adrenaline]]. Adrenaline is known to cause physical symptoms that accompany test anxiety, such as increased heart rate, sweating, and rapid breathing.<ref>{{cite web|last=Lyness|first=D'Arcy|title=Test Anxiety|url= http://kidshealth.org/teen/school_jobs/school/test_anxiety.html|work=The Nemours Foundation.|accessdate=4 April 2012}}</ref> In many cases having adrenaline is a good thing. It is helpful when dealing with stressful situations, ensuring alertness and preparation;<ref>Cohen S., Kozlovsky N., Matar M.A., Kaplan Z., Zohar J. and Cohen H. (2012). [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3442354/ Post-exposure sleep deprivation facilitates correctly-timed interactions between glucocorticoid and adrenergic systems which attenuate traumatic stress responses]. ''Neuropsychopharmacology'' 37; 2388–2404</ref> but for some people, the symptoms are difficult or impossible to handle, making it impossible to focus on tests.

Test anxiety consists of:

*'''Physiological overarousal''' – often termed ''[[emotionality]]''.  [[Somatic symptom disorder|Somatic]] signs include headaches, stomach aches, nausea, [[diarrhea]], excessive sweating, shortness of breath, light-headedness or fainting, rapid heartbeat and dry mouth. Test anxiety can also lead to panic attacks, in which the student may have a sudden intense fear, difficulty breathing, and extreme discomfort.
*'''Worry and dread''' – maladaptive cognitions. This includes catastrophic expectations of gloom and doom, fear of failure, random thoughts, feelings of inadequacy, self-condemnation, negative self-talk, frustration and comparing oneself unfavorably to others.
*'''Cognitive/Behavioral''' – poor concentration, "going blank" or "freezing," confusion, and poor organization.  The inability to concentrate leads to impaired performance on tests. Fidgeting during or outright avoidance of the test. Students often report "blanking out" even though they have studied sufficiently for the test.<ref name="New York Times Company">{{cite web|last=Cherry|first=Kendra|title=Test Anxiety Symptoms|url=http://psychology.about.com/od/mentalhealth/a/test-anxiety-symptoms.htm|work=About.com|accessdate=24 April 2012|archive-date=1 December 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111201181000/http://psychology.about.com/od/mentalhealth/a/test-anxiety-symptoms.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>
*'''Emotional''' – low self-esteem, depression, anger, and a feeling of hopelessness.<ref name="New York Times Company"/>

==Causes==
Research shows that parental pressure is associated with greater worry, test irrelevant thoughts, and stronger bodily symptoms relating to anxiety during a test.<ref name="Putwain"/>

Other causes of test anxiety may include fear of failure, [[procrastination]], and previous poor test performance.<ref>{{cite web|last=ADAA|title=Test Anxiety|url=http://www.adaa.org/living-with-anxiety/children/test-anxiety|work=Anxiety Disorder Association of America|accessdate=26 April 2012}}</ref> As well, characteristics of the test environment such as: nature of the task, difficulty, atmosphere, time constraints, examiner characteristics, mode of administration and physical setting can affect the level of anxiousness felt by the student.<ref name= "Salend"/><ref name="Putwain"/> Researchers Putwain & Best (2011),<ref name="Best">Putwain D.W., Best, N. (2011). Fear appeals in the primary classroom: effects on test anxiety and test grade. Learning and Individual Differences, 21 580-584</ref> examined test performance among elementary children when the teacher put pressure on the students in an attempt to create a more high stress environment. Their findings showed that students performed worse in high threat situations and experienced more test anxiety and worrisome thoughts than when in a low threat environment.

Test anxiety is known to develop into a vicious cycle. After experiencing test anxiety on one test, the student may become so fearful of it happening again they become more anxious and upset than they would normally, or even than they experienced on the previous test. If the cycle continues without acknowledgement, or the student seeking help, the student may begin to feel helpless in the situation.<ref>{{cite web|last=Cherry|first=Kendra|title=Causes of Test Anxiety|url=http://psychology.about.com/od/mentalhealth/a/test-anxiety-causes.htm|work=The New York Times Company|accessdate=24 April 2012|archive-date=17 April 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120417100418/http://psychology.about.com/od/mentalhealth/a/test-anxiety-causes.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

People who experience test anxiety often have parents or siblings who have test anxiety or other types of anxiety. Anxiety does seem to have some genetic components.<ref>{{cite web|last=Rodriguez|first=Diana|title=Overcoming College Anxiety|url=http://www.everydayhealth.com/college-health/overcoming-college-test-anxiety.aspx|work=Everyday Health|accessdate=4 April 2012}}</ref>

===Diagnosis===

Test anxiety can be diagnosed using the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual-IV, under the classification of ''social phobia.''<ref name=McDonald />
Social phobias are characterized by ''a marked and persistent fear of social or performance situations in which embarrassment may occur''. In order to be diagnosed as suffering from a social phobia, the DSM-IV states that the individual must present four different factors.<ref name=McDonald />

*Must show an immediate anxiety response when exposed to the feared social or performance situation.
*Must show various attempts to avoid social or performance situation, or sometimes endure it but with extreme fear. 
*Must experience a  disruption to normal activities due to the avoidance or fear associated with the situation
*Must have experienced the symptoms for at least six months.<ref name=McDonald />

Other variables related to test anxiety are:

*[[Obsessive compulsive disorder]]s
*Perfectionist tendencies and unrealistic expectations
*Negative [[self-esteem]], self-statements, and criticism
*Poor motivation or lack of confidence
*[[Stereotype threat]]
*Inadequate study and test-taking skills
*Poor eating, sleeping and exercising habits<ref>{{cite web|title=Health, Exercise, Diet, Rest, Self-Image, Motivation, and Attitudes|url=http://www.muskingum.edu/~cal/database/general/physiopsyc.html|publisher=Muskingum College|accessdate=8 April 2013}}</ref>{{additional citation needed |date=June 2016}}

==Theories==

Anxiety is defined as the "psychological mechanism whereby the current intensification of a dangerous drive results in the elicitation of defenses."<ref>Rosenwald, G.C (1961). [https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1962-06548-001 The assessment of anxiety in psychological experimentation: a theoretical reformulation and test]. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 62(3): 666-673</ref> George Mandler and Seymour Sarason (1952), developed the theory that anxiety present in testing situations is an important determinant of test performance.  Individuals that become highly anxious during tests typically perform more poorly on tests than low-test anxious persons, especially when tests are given under stressful evaluative conditions such as a post-secondary exam. The feelings of forgetfulness, or drawing a "blank" are developed because of anxiety-produced interference between relevant responses and irrelevant responses generated from the person's anxious state. The difference in performance of a high-anxious test taker compared to a low-anxious test taker is largely due to the difference in their ability to focus on the tasks required.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Wine | first1 = J | year = 1971 | title = Test anxiety and direction of attention | journal = Psychological Bulletin | volume = 76 | issue = 2| pages = 92–104 | doi=10.1037/h0031332| pmid = 4937878 | s2cid = 3826188 }}</ref> A low-anxious test taker is able to focus greater attention on the tasks required of them while taking the test, while a high-anxious test taker is focused on their internal self, and the anxiety they are feeling. Anxious test takers do not perform adequately on the test as their attention is divided between themselves and the test. Therefore, students with high test anxiety are unable to focus their full attention on the test. Furthermore, anxiousness is evoked when a student believes that the evaluative situation, such as an assessment, exceeds his or her intellectual, motivational, and social capabilities.<ref name= "Putwain">Putwain, D.W., Woods, K.A., Symes, W. (2010). [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1348/000709909X466082 Personal and situational predictors of test anxiety of students in post-compulsory education]. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 80, 137-160</ref>

Psychologists Liebert and Morris (1967) analyzed the structure of test anxiety given on two distinct factors: ''Cognitive Test Anxiety'' and ''Emotionality''.<ref name="Cassady & Johnson" /> '''''Emotionality''''' means that the individual shows high levels of several different symptoms related to test anxiety that can be seen through physiological responses experienced during situations where they are being evaluated; such as an exam.<ref name="Cassady & Johnson" /> Some of the physiological manifestations include: increased galvanic skin response and heart rate, dizziness, nausea, or feelings of panic.<ref name="Cassady & Johnson" /> There is evidence that emotionality is a distinct part of test anxiety; however, it can be seen that when an individual displays high emotionality it means that it is mostly associated with declining performance, but only when the individual is also experiencing high levels of worry.<ref name="Cassady & Johnson" />

The other factor mentioned is '''''Cognitive Test Anxiety''''', also known as worry. It is mostly composed of the individuals cognitive reactions to situations where they are being evaluated, in the times prior to, during, and after those tasks.<ref name="Cassady & Johnson" /> Some of the thoughts that individuals with high cognitive test anxiety are constantly dealing with are comparing self performance to peers, considering the consequences of failure, low levels of confidence in performance, excessive worry about grades, feeling that they are unprepared for tests, and loss of self-worth.<ref name="Cassady & Johnson" />

Researchers Putwain, Woods & Symes (2010), found that a low academic [[self-concept]] was associated with higher worry and tension about their abilities to do well on a test. A student's metacognitive beliefs play an important role in the maintenance of negative self-beliefs.<ref name="Putwain"/>

Anxiety reactions can be generalized from previous experiences to testing situations.<ref>Mandler, G. & Sarson, S. B. (1952). A study of anxiety and learning. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 47, 166-173</ref> Feelings of inadequacy, helplessness, anticipations of punishment or loss of status and esteem manifest anxiety responses. As well, the presence of an audience can debilitate the performance of high anxious test takers and increase the performance of low anxious test takers. Persons who score high on anxiety scales tend to describe themselves in negative, self-devaluing terms. Highly anxious test takers also blame themselves for their failure significantly more than low anxious test takers.

The study of the relationship between  anxiety and performance can be understood by using the '''Yerkes-Dodson Law,''' where one can see the facilitating and debilitating effects of arousal on performance as an inverted "U".<ref name=McDonald /> 
An example of this correlation can be seen in terms of a child taking a test where the degree of arousal or anxiety that the child portrays can be seen as beneficial to the performance. Though, if the child doesn't have a feeling or fear or failure or some sort of encouragement to perform well on the test, then the child is unlikely to put the necessary effort into preparing or being motivated when taking the test and so he or she will not perform to their fullest potential.<ref name=McDonald />

However, if before or during a test a child's level of anxiety is above the optimum level, they may also fail to demonstrate their true abilities.<ref name=McDonald /> Under these circumstances fear of the actual test may disrupt preparation and cause a great amount of distress during the test that it is more than likely to impair their performance.<ref name=McDonald />

===Attentional theories===
There are two main groups of attentional theories that attempt to explain compromised performance in pressured situations.<ref name = DeCaro>{{cite journal | url=http://hpl.uchicago.edu/Publications/Choking%20Under%20Pressure%20Multiple%20Routes%20to%20Skill%20Failure.pdf | title=Choking under pressure: multiple routes to skill failure. |vauthors=DeCaro MS, Thomas RD, Albert NB, Beilock SL | journal=J Exp Psychol Gen |date=August 2011 | volume=140 | issue=3 | pages=390–406 | doi=10.1037/a0023466| pmid=21574739 }}</ref>

One group of theories are the ''explicit monitoring theories''. They state that when a person is expected to perform a specific skill, the pressure may cause an increased self-consciousness and inward focus, which can disrupt their ability to successfully perform that task.<ref name = interplay/> Thinking about step-by-step procedures can inhibit one's ability to execute a task.<ref name = DeCaro/> For example, a study by R. Gray found that baseball players put into the high-pressure condition had increased errors, and an increased ability to recall details like the direction their bat was moving.  This indicates that the pressured players were monitoring themselves more, which impacted their ability to successfully hit the ball.<ref name = DeCaro/>

A second group of theories are the ''distraction theories''. These theories state that high-pressure environments create a dual-task situation, in which the person's attention is divided between the task at hand and unhelpful thoughts about the situation and possible negative consequences of poor performance.<ref name = interplay>[http://home.uchicago.edu/ramirezg/CH05.pdf On the interplay of emotion and cognitive control: Implications for enhancing academic achievement.]  Beilock, Sian L. Ramirez, Gerardo; In: The psychology of learning and motivation (Vol 55): Cognition in education. Mestre, Jose P. (Ed.); Ross, Brian H. (Ed.); San Diego, CA, US: Elsevier Academic Press, Vol 55, 2011. pp. 140-141</ref> 
Attention is an important part of [[working memory]],<ref name = interplay/> which is the system that actively holds several pieces of relevant information in the mind while inhibiting irrelevant information.<ref name = interplay/> Working memory has a limited capacity, and the addition of stress and anxiety reduces the resources available to focus on relevant information.<ref name = Revlin>Revlin, Russell. Cognition: Theory and Practice. New York, NY: Worth, 2013. Print.</ref>

In situations in which individuals need to concentrate their attention on a specific task, emotional stimuli can divert their attention to a greater degree than non-emotional stimuli.<ref>{{cite journal | title=Attentional capture by emotional stimuli is preserved in patients with amygdala lesions | author=Richard M. Piech, Maureen McHugo, Stephen D. Smith, Mildred S. Dukic, Joost Van Der Meer, Bassel Abou-Khalil, Steven B. Most and David H. Zald | journal=Neuropsychologia |date=October 2011 | volume=49 | issue=12 | pages=3314–3319 | doi=10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2011.08.004 | pmc=3192286 | pmid=21884712}}</ref> Emotional stimuli will often dominate a person's thoughts, and any attempt to suppress them will require additional working memory resources.<ref name = Revlin/> When working memory divides resources between the aversive cognitions and the task-relevant material, then the person's ability to use the relevant information on a test will suffer.<ref name = Mowbray>{{cite journal |doi=10.1017/edp.2012.16|title=Working Memory, Test Anxiety and Effective Interventions: A Review|journal=The Australian Educational and Developmental Psychologist|volume=29|issue=2|pages=141–156|year=2012|last1=Mowbray|first1=Tony|s2cid=144367873 }}</ref><br />People who suffer from test anxiety are more likely to experience negative cognitions while in evaluative situations. Furthermore, test anxious persons have been found to bias their attention towards threatening and anxiety related stimuli more than nonemotional stimuli.<ref name = Baddeley2013>{{cite journal |doi=10.1037/a0030029|title=Working memory and emotion: Ruminations on a theory of depression|journal=Review of General Psychology|volume=17|pages=20–27|year=2013|last1=Baddeley|first1=Alan|citeseerx=10.1.1.400.9070|s2cid=146937622}}</ref><br />Research has accordingly found that tasks that rely heavily on working memory are the ones that suffer the most during pressure.<ref name = interplay/> Shortfalls in performance that are caused by test anxiety seem to be related to the extent to which the student has full access to their [[working memory]].<ref>{{cite journal | title=Test anxiety and Working Memory | author=Ju Hyun Lee | journal=Journal of Experimental Education | year=1999 | volume=67 | issue=3 | pages=218–240 | doi=10.1080/00220979909598354|jstor = 20152597}}</ref>

When comparing these two theories in the context of academic performance, a majority of work supports distraction theories.<ref name = interplay/> One reason for this is that many of the skills performed in the classroom require heavy demands on working memory.<ref name = interplay/> However, there are different kinds of pressure situations. There is ''monitoring pressure'', in which an individual's performance is impacted due to the presence of an audience, and ''outcome pressure'', in which an individual's performance is influenced by the consequences of the testing results.<ref name = DeCaro/> In a study, DeCaro ''et al.'' found that performance on a rule-based task, that relies heavily on working memory, was impaired by outcome pressure, but not monitoring pressure, whereas performance on an information-integration task, which does not require [[attentional control]], was hurt by monitoring pressure, but not outcome pressure.<ref name = DeCaro/> These findings indicate that  performance is compromised in different ways depending on the type of task, and the types of pressure, and that both theories can be correct.<ref name = DeCaro/>

====Attentional control====
[[File:Baddley's Model of Working Memory.png|thumbnail|Schematic of the four elements of Baddeley's model of working memory]]
[[Michael Eysenck|Eysenck]] ''et al.''<ref>Eysenck, M. W., Santos, R., Derekshan, N., & Calvo, M. G. (2007). Anxiety and cognitive performance: Attentional Control Theory. Emotion, 7(2), 336–352.</ref> elaborate upon the distraction theories and propose the attentional control theory.<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://www.k-state.edu/psych/research/documents/Rai_et_al_2010-online_Effects_of_Stress_and_WM_Capacity_on_FL_Readers_Inferential_Proc_Durin.pdf | title=Effects of Stress and Working Memory Capacity on Foreign Language Readers' Inferential Processing During Comprehension |author1=Manpreet K. Rai |author2=Lester C. Loschky |author3=Richard Jackson Harris |author4=Nicole R. Peck |author5=Lindsay G. Cook | journal=Language Learning |date=March 2011 | volume=61 | issue=1 | pages=187–218 | doi=10.1111/j.1467-9922.2010.00592.x}}</ref> This theory uses [[Baddeley's model of working memory]] to explain the effects of anxiety on working memory and on performance.<ref name = Derakshan/> In Baddeley's theory, working memory (WM) consists of four components, one of them the [[central executive]] that has a number of tasks such as coordination of the temporary stores of phonological and visual information ([[phonological loop]] and [[visuospatial sketchpad]], respectively).<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1016/S1364-6613(00)01538-2 | last1 = Baddeley | first1 = A.D. | year = 2000 | title = The episodic buffer: A new component of working memory? | journal = Trends in Cognitive Sciences | volume = 4 | issue = 11| pages = 417–423 | pmid=11058819| s2cid = 14333234 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

The attentional control theory assumes that anxiety primarily affects attentional control, which is a key function of the central executive.<ref name = Derakshan/> Attentional control is the balance between the two attentional systems, the ''goal-directed system'', influenced by the individual's goals, and the ''stimulus-driven system'', influenced by salient stimuli.<ref name = Derakshan/> According to the attentional control theory, anxiety disrupts the balance between these two systems. The stimulus-driven system becomes stronger at the expense of the goal-directed system, thereby impairing the efficiency of the inhibition and shifting functions of the central executive.<ref name = Derakshan/>

In support of this theory, there is strong evidence that anxiety largely impairs processing efficiency rather than performance effectiveness.<ref name = Derakshan>{{cite journal |doi=10.1027/1016-9040.14.2.168|title=Anxiety, Processing Efficiency, and Cognitive Performance|journal=European Psychologist|volume=14|issue=2|pages=168–176|year=2009|last1=Derakshan|first1=Nazanin|last2=Eysenck|first2=Michael W.|s2cid=17683537}}</ref> Performance effectiveness refers to the quality of performance whereas processing efficiency refers to the amount of resources used to attain an effective performance.<ref name = Derakshan/> There is also evidence that anxiety impairs both the inhibition and the shifting function.<ref name = Derakshan/> Therefore, this theory suggests that students high in test anxiety will have to allocate more resources to the task at hand than non-test anxiety students in order to achieve the same results.<ref name = Mowbray/>

In general, people with higher working memory capacity do better on academic tasks, but this changes when people are under acute pressure.<ref name = interplay/> [[Sian Beilock]] ''et al.'' found that pressure led individuals with a high working memory capacity to perform worse on a complicated task, whereas individuals with a low WM capacity got the same low results with or without pressure. This was because people with high WM could use more effective, but more demanding, [[problem solving]] strategies in the low pressure condition, which they had to abandon in the high pressure condition. The low WM people never used these demanding strategies in the first place.<ref name = interplay/> Evidence for similar working memory effects in children has also been found.<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1111/bjep.12027 | last1 = Wang | first1 = Z. | year = 2013 | title = The effect of pressure on high- and low-working-memory students: An elaboration of the choking under pressure hypothesis | url =https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/106943/1/bjep12027.pdf | journal = British Journal of Educational Psychology| volume =  84| issue = 2| pages = 1–13 | pmid=24164334| hdl = 2027.42/106943 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> Evidence that trait anxiety might have different effects on working memory than state or acute pressure situations comes from Johnson ''et al.'' who found individuals' performances on a task showed a decrease in accuracy due to trait anxiety for individuals with low or average WM capacity, but did not significantly decrease for individuals with high WM.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/10615800802291277|pmid=18785033|title=Individuals lower in working memory capacity are particularly vulnerable to anxiety's disruptive effect on performance|journal=Anxiety, Stress & Coping|volume=22|issue=2|pages=201–213|year=2009|last1=Johnson|first1=Dan R.|last2=Gronlund|first2=Scott D.|s2cid=25492130}}</ref>

==Measurement scales==

Early scales, by authors such as [[Charles Spielberger]], tended to focus on physiological and somatic features and on worry, commonly referred to as ''emotionality'',<ref>cf Charles Spielberger</ref> while more recent offerings, such as that by Cassady & Johnson, emphasize cognitive processes.<ref name="Cassady2001">Cassady, J. & Johnson, R. (2001). Cognitive test anxiety and academic performance. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 27, 270–295.</ref> "Test anxiety" for these authors consists of physiological and mental processes, and impaired test performance is seen as the result.

The ''Children's Test Anxiety Questionnaire'' is specifically designed to measure test anxiety in children 8–12 years of age. It provides scores for three dimensions of test anxiety: "worrisome thoughts concerning failure (i.e. 'when I take tests, I worry about failing'), automatic reactions concerning students' general and specific somatic indications of anxiety (i.e. 'when I take tests, my heart beats fast'), and off-task behaviours concerning nervous habits and distracting behaviours (i.e. 'when I take tests, I play with my pencil')" <ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/10615800412331292606|title=Measuring test anxiety in children: Scale development and internal construct validation|journal=Anxiety, Stress & Coping|volume=17|issue=3|pages=227–240|year=2004|last1=Wren|first1=Douglas G.|last2=Benson|first2=Jeri|s2cid=19022641}}</ref>

The ''Test Anxiety Inventory for Children and Adolescent'' (TAICA) is a way to measure and assess test anxiety in children and adolescents in Grades 4 through 12. Those individuals who are being assessed rate their responses on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (never true about me) to 5 (always true about me). The TAICA is a 45-item self-report measure which consists of four sub scales.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lowe|first1=Patricia A.|last2=Lee|first2=Steven W.|last3=Witteborg|first3=Kristin M.|last4=Prichard|first4=Keri W.|last5=Luhr|first5=Megan E.|last6=Cullinan|first6=Christopher M.|last7=Mildren|first7=Bethany A|last8=Raad|first8=Jennifer M.|last9=Cornelius|first9=Rebecca A.|last10=Janik|first10=Melissa|title=Examination of the Psychometric Properties of a New Multidimensional Measure of Test Anxiety Among Elementary and Secondary School Students|journal=Psychoeducational Assessment|date=September 2008|volume=26|issue=3|pages=215–230|doi=10.1177/0734282907303760|s2cid=143100124}}</ref>

*Cognitive Obstruction/Inattention subscale assesses memory and attention difficulties and obstructed cognitions associated with test anxiety
*Physiological Hyperarousal subscale measures physical symptoms associated with the test-taking process.
*Social Humiliation subscale measures fear associated with failing a test and being belittled or ridiculed by significant others
*Worry subscale assesses negative thoughts and worries that adversely affect test performance.

==Treatment ==
Medication is not recommended to treat test anxiety; instead, standard suggestions include sleep, proper nutrition, exercise, meditation, studying without stress, and enacting habits to reduce stress during the test.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sawchuk |first1=Craig |title=Test anxiety: Can it be treated? |url=https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/generalized-anxiety-disorder/expert-answers/test-anxiety/faq-20058195 |website=Mayo Clinic}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Downs |first1=Cecilia |title=Managing Test Anxiety |url=https://www.brown.edu/campus-life/support/counseling-and-psychological-services/index.php?q=managing-test-anxiety |website=Brown University Counseling and Psychological Services}}</ref>
Test anxiety remains a challenge for students and has considerable physiological and psychological impacts. The routine practice of slow, Device-Guided Breathing (DGB) is a
major component of behavioral treatments for anxiety conditions.<ref>{{cite web|author=Ovadia-Blechman Z, Tarrasch R, Velicki M, Chalutz Ben-Gal H. (2022)|title=Reducing Test Anxiety by Device-Guided Breathing: A Pilot Study|url=https://english.afeka.ac.il/media/2235899/frintiers-in-psychology-2022.pdf|publisher=Frontiers in Psychology 23 (13), 2022|access-date=2022-07-27|archive-date=2022-10-09|archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221009/https://english.afeka.ac.il/media/2235899/frintiers-in-psychology-2022.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Management===
To gain an accurate assessment of student comprehension, instructors should be concerned with minimizing the effects of test anxiety. Instructors might offer "second chances" post test, familiarize students with test format and grading scheme, and lower the impact of any one test.<ref>Wilbert J. Mckeachie and Marilla Svinicki's "Teaching Tips" 12th edition, pg. 110;</ref> If students have greater confidence in their test-taking skills, they are more likely to be comfortable and relaxed when the testing does occur. Having an intentional thinking strategy should help student performance improve.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Parks-Stamm |first1=Elizabeth J. |last2=Gollwitzer |first2=Peter M. |last3=Oettingen |first3=Gabriele |title=Implementation intentions and test anxiety: Shielding academic performance from distraction |journal=Learning and Individual Differences |date=2010 |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=30–33 |doi=10.1016/j.lindif.2009.09.001}}</ref>

For some individuals, poor academic performance is due to skill deficits, which could include problems in encoding (learning), rehearsal (study skills) or retrieval during a test (test-taking strategies).<ref>Damer, D.E., Melendres, L.T (2011). [https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01933922.2011.586016 Tackling Test Anxiety: A groups for college students]. The Journal for Specialists in Group Work, 36(3):163-177</ref> Skill deficits may lead to poor performance directly (failure to adequately learn the material) or indirectly (awareness of being ill-prepared causes anxiety that, in turn, leads to poor performance). Therefore, the most effective interventions are those that combine skill-focused strategies (i.e. study skills training, test-taking skills) with cognitive (i.e. cognitive restructuring) or behavioural approaches (i.e. relaxation training, systematic desensitization).<ref>Ergene, T. (2003). Effective interventions on test anxiety reduction. School Psychology International, 24, 313–328</ref>

Students also need to stay healthy in order to be able to deal with stress and anxiety. They need to eat healthy, and get enough sleep.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.health.harvard.edu/blog/eating-well-to-help-manage-anxiety-your-questions-answered-2018031413460|title=Eating well to help manage anxiety: Your questions answered - Harvard Health Blog|last=MD|first=Uma Naidoo|date=2018-03-14|work=Harvard Health Blog|access-date=2018-10-14|language=en-US}}</ref>

ARTICLE: Test preparation

{{Short description|Preparation for standardized tests}}
{{Original research|date=June 2009}}
[[File:Four Tulane University Students Studying January 2008.jpg|thumb|A group of students preparing for a test|248x248px]]
'''Test preparation''' (abbreviated '''test prep''') or '''exam preparation''' is an educational course, [[tutoring]] service, educational material, or a learning tool designed to increase [[student]]s' performance on [[standardized test]]s. Examples of these tests include [[entrance examination]]s used for admissions to institutions of [[higher education]], such as [[college admission|college]] (e.g. the [[SAT]] and [[ACT (test)|ACT]]), [[business school]] (the [[GMAT]]), [[law school]] (the [[LSAT]] or [[LNAT]]), [[medical school]] (the [[MCAT]], [[BMAT]], [[University Clinical Aptitude Test|UCAT]] and [[GAMSAT]]) and [[graduate school]] (the [[Graduate Record Examination|GRE]]) and qualifying examinations for admission to [[gifted education]] programs.<ref name="NYT021713">{{cite news|title=Schools Ask: Gifted or Just Well-Prepared?|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/02/18/nyregion/new-york-city-schools-struggle-to-separate-the-gifted-from-the-just-well-prepared.html|access-date=February 28, 2013|newspaper=The New York Times|date=February 17, 2013|author=Jenny Anderson}}</ref>

== Preparation options ==
There are many resources and services on which students may draw as they prepare for standardized tests, including: 
* [[Course (education)|Courses]]: Many test preparation courses are designed to expose students to the breadth of topics tested on the relevant exam and guide them through the process of studying.
* [[Flashcard]]s: Index cards imprinted with information used as a study aid to reinforce memory retention.
* [[Mind map|Mind maps]]: Mind maps allow students to visually organize relevant concepts and information, showing relationships among pieces of the whole.<ref>{{Cite book|chapter=Exam Tips|last=Smart|first=Ursulua|title=Criminal Justice |publisher=SAGE Publications Ltd|year=2006|pages=162–166|doi=10.4135/9781446212127.n22|isbn=978-1-4129-0707-1 }}</ref>
*{{anchor|Mock}}Mock exams: Mock examinations help students prepare for the real exams. They are intended to give students a clear indication of the structure and content of the actual exam and experience of examination conditions, whilst also offering them a snapshot of their current performance.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/teacher-network/2015/dec/03/practice-makes-perfect-why-mock-exams-students-brains|title=Practice makes perfect: why mock exams are great for students' brains|last=Busch|first=Bradley|date=2015-12-03|website=The Guardian|access-date=2016-05-17}}</ref>
* [[Study group]]s: Studying as group facilitates collaboration and exposes students to different perspectives on the material.<ref>{{Cite book|chapter=Exam tips|last=Smartt|first=Ursulua|title=Criminal Justice |publisher=SAGE Publications Ltd|year=2006|pages=162–166|doi=10.4135/9781446212127.n22|isbn=978-1-4129-0707-1 }}</ref>
* [[Study guide|Study guides]]: Various organizations and individuals produce published materials that students can incorporate into their preparation. 
* [[Tutor]]s: A tutor is a person with whom students work one-on-one to improve academic performance, in this case on an exam.

==Resource providers==
Most companies and educators that offer test preparation services also offer traditional (hard copy) such as books and printed materials and technology or online-based learning tools, such as content accessible on hand-held devices such as smartphones, tablets and laptops. So do most test makers, publishers of self-help, instructional and educational materials, and makers of hardware and software.

===Test makers===
* [[ACT (test)|ACT, Inc.]] - publisher of the [[ACT (test)|ACT]]
* [[American Council on Education]] (ACE) - publisher of the [[GED]] test 
* [[Association of American Medical Colleges|Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC)]] - publisher of the [[MCAT]] test
* [[College Board]] - publisher of the [[SAT]] test
* [[Educational Testing Service|Educational Testing Service (ETS)]] - publisher of the [[Graduate Record Examinations|GRE]] and [[TOEFL]] tests
* [[Elsevier]] - publisher of the [[HESI_exam | HESI]] exam
* [[Graduate Management Admission Council|Graduate Management Admission Council (GMAC)]] - publisher of the [[GMAT]]
* [[Harcourt Assessment]] - publisher of the [[Miller Analogies Test]] (MAT)
* [[Law School Admissions Council]] (LSAC) - publisher of the [[LSAT]] test
* [[National Restaurant Association]] - publisher of the [[ServSafe]]

===Third parties===
* [[Barron's Educational Series]] - publisher of books and educational materials
* [[CliffsNotes]] - publisher of study guides
* The [[Complete Idiot's Guides]] - publisher of instructional reference books
* [[For Dummies]] - publisher of instructional/reference books 
* [[Gary Gruber]] - educator and author
* [[McGraw-Hill]] - publisher of books and educational materials 
* [[Peterson's]] - publisher of books and educational materials
* [[SparkNotes]] - publisher of study guides
* [[Study Notes]] - publisher of study guides
* [[Texas Instruments]] - technology company that offers test-maker approved calculators and a variety of test preparation and test-taking tools
* [[Www.nursenest.ca|NurseNest]] - a company that provides test preparation for nursing students in Canada/United States 

==Criticism==
Some test-preparation programs have been proven to help students improve test scores,<ref>[[American Book Company (1996)|American Book Company]] [http://www.americanbookcompany.com/valstudy.html Validation Study] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110222034256/http://www.americanbookcompany.com/valstudy.html |date=2011-02-22 }}</ref> but others may have little effect.

* [[Cram school]]
