{{Short description|Full immersion in an activity}}
{{Redirect|Flow state|other uses|Flow State (disambiguation)}}
{{AI-generated|partial=y|date=February 2026|reason=Text added in [[Special:Diff/1167941571|this 2023 edit]]; note [[WP:AISIGNS]] in superficial analyses, vocab distribution typical of 2023 LLMs, title case etc}}
[[File:Scout Girl in Concentration.jpg|thumb|right|alt=A girl with long brown hair concentrates on threading pink string though white string, on a sports field|Concentrating on a task, one aspect of flow]]

'''Flow''' in [[positive psychology]], also known colloquially as being '''in''' '''the zone''' or focused, is the [[mental state]] in which a person performing some activity is fully immersed in a feeling of energized [[Attention|focus]], full involvement, and enjoyment in the process of the activity. In essence, flow is characterized by the complete absorption in what one does, and a resulting transformation in one's sense of time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ellis |first1=Gary D. |last2=Voelkl |first2=Judith E. |last3=Morris |first3=Catherine |date=September 1994 |title=Measurement and Analysis Issues with Explanation of Variance in Daily Experience Using the Flow Model |journal=Journal of Leisure Research |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=337–356 |doi=10.1080/00222216.1994.11969966 |bibcode=1994JLeiR..26..337E |issn=0022-2216}}</ref> Flow is the melting together of action and [[consciousness]]; the state of finding a balance between a skill and how challenging that task is. It requires a high level of concentration. Flow is used as a [[coping]] skill for stress and anxiety when productively pursuing a form of leisure that matches one's skill set.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mirvis |first=Philip H. |date=July 1991 |title=Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience, by Csikszentmihalyi Michael. New York: Harper & Row, 1990, 303 pp., $19.95, cloth. |journal=Academy of Management Review |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=636–640 |doi=10.5465/amr.1991.4279513 |issn=0363-7425}}</ref>

First presented in the 1975 book ''Beyond Boredom and Anxiety'' by the [[Hungarians|Hungarian]]-American psychologist [[Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi|Mihály Csíkszentmihályi]],{{sfnp|Csikszentmihályi|1975|pp=11-12,36-37}}<ref>{{harvnb|Csikszentmihályi|1990|p=242}}: "The original research and the theoretical model of the flow experience were first fully reported in ''Beyond Boredom and Anxiety'' (Csikszentmihalyi 1975)."</ref> the concept has been widely referred to across a variety of fields (and is particularly well recognized in [[occupational therapy]]).

The flow state shares many characteristics with [[hyperfocus]].<ref name="doi.org">{{Cite journal |last1=Ashinoff |first1=Brandon K. |last2=Abu-Akel |first2=Ahmad |date=2021-02-01 |title=Hyperfocus: the forgotten frontier of attention |journal=Psychological Research |language=en |volume=85 |issue=1 |pages=1–19 |doi=10.1007/s00426-019-01245-8 |issn=1430-2772 |pmc=7851038 |pmid=31541305}}</ref> However, hyperfocus is not always described in a positive light. Some examples include spending "too much" time playing video games or becoming pleasurably absorbed by one aspect of an assignment or task to the detriment of the overall assignment. In some cases, hyperfocus can "capture" a person, perhaps causing them to appear unfocused or to start several unfinished [[project]]s. Hyperfocus is often mentioned "in the context of [[autism]], [[schizophrenia]], and [[attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]] – conditions that have consequences on attentional abilities."<ref name="doi.org"/>

Flow is an individual experience and the idea behind flow originated from the [[sport psychology]] theory about an Individual Zone of Optimal Functioning. The individuality of the concept of flow suggests that each person has their subjective area of flow, where they would function best given the situation. One is most likely to experience flow at moderate levels of psychological [[arousal]], as one is unlikely to be overwhelmed, but not understimulated to the point of boredom.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sanderson |first=Catherine |title=Sport Psychology |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2016 |isbn=978-0-19-991744-0 |pages=164–165}}</ref>

==Etymology==
Flow is so named because, during Csíkszentmihályi's 1975 interviews, several people described their "flow" experiences using the metaphor of a water current carrying them along:
{{Blockquote|
We have called this state the flow experience, because this is the term many of the people we interviewed had used in their descriptions of how it felt to be in top form: "It was like floating," "I was carried on by the flow."
|author=Csikszentmihályi
|source=Flow (1990){{sfnp|Csikszentmihályi|1990|p=40}}
}}

==History==
[[Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi|Mihaly Csikszentmihályi]] and others began researching flow after he became fascinated by artists who would essentially get lost in their work.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barrett |first=Nathaniel F. |date=2011 |title=''Wuwei'' and Flow: Comparative Reflections on Spirituality, Transcendence, and Skill in the ''Zhuangzi'' |url=http://enlight.lib.ntu.edu.tw/FULLTEXT/JR-PHIL/phil390582.pdf |journal=Philosophy East and West |volume=61 |issue=4 |pages=679–706 |doi=10.1353/pew.2011.0051 |issn=1529-1898 |s2cid=56222168 |s2cid-access=free |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170810124108/http://enlight.lib.ntu.edu.tw/FULLTEXT/JR-PHIL/phil390582.pdf |archive-date= Aug 10, 2017 }}</ref> Artists, especially painters, got so immersed in their work that they would disregard their need for food, water and even sleep. The theory of flow came about when Csikszentmihályi tried to understand the phenomenon experienced by these artists. Flow research became prevalent in the 1980s and 1990s, with Csikszentmihályi and his colleagues in Italy still at the forefront. Researchers grew interested in optimal experiences and emphasizing positive experiences, especially in places such as schools and the business world.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Flow and the Foundations of Positive Psychology The Collected Works of Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi |url=https://www.academia.edu/39728351 |first1=Mihaly |last1=Csikszentmihalyi |date=2014 |isbn=978-94-017-9083-3 |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-9088-8 |publisher=Springer |via=Academia.edu }}</ref> They also began studying the theory of flow at this time.<ref name="Nakamura_2001" />

The [[cognitive science]] of flow has been studied under the rubric of effortless attention.<ref>{{cite book |title=Effortless Attention: A New Perspective in the Cognitive Science of Attention and action |date=2010 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-26943-8 |veditors=Bruya B |series=Bradford Book |location=Cambridge, Mass. |oclc=646069518}}</ref>

==Components==
Jeanne Nakamura and Csíkszentmihályi identify the following six factors as encompassing an experience of flow:<ref name="Nakamura_2001">{{cite book | vauthors = Nakamura J, Csikszentmihályi M |author-link2=Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi | veditors = Snyder CR, Lopez SJ | editor1-link = Charles R. Snyder   | date=20 December 2001 |title=Handbook of Positive Psychology |chapter=Flow Theory and Research |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-803094-2 |pages=195–206 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2Cr5rP8jOnsC |access-date=20 November 2013}}</ref>

# Intense and focused [[Attentional control|concentration]] on [[the present]] moment
# Merging of [[Action (philosophy)|action]] and [[awareness]]
# A loss of [[Self-reflection#Modern era|reflective]] [[self-consciousness]]
# A sense of personal control or agency over the situation or activity
# A distortion of temporal experience, as one's [[sense of time|subjective experience of time]] is altered
# Experience of the activity as intrinsically [[Reward system|rewarding]], also referred to as [[wiktionary:autotelic|autotelic]] experience

Those aspects can appear independently of each other, but only in combination do they constitute a so-called ''flow experience''. Additionally, psychology writer Kendra Cherry has mentioned three other components that Csíkszentmihályi lists as being a part of the flow experience:<ref name="Cherry_2014">{{cite web | vauthors = Cherry K |date= 8 September 2014 |title=What is Flow? |website=About Education |url=http://psychology.about.com/od/PositivePsychology/a/flow.htm |access-date=30 March 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150403200155/http://psychology.about.com/od/PositivePsychology/a/flow.htm |archive-date=April 3, 2015}}</ref>
# Immediate feedback
# Feeling the potential to succeed
# Feeling so engrossed in the experience that other needs become negligible
Just as with the conditions listed above, these conditions can be independent of one another.

In 2021, Cameron Norsworthy and colleagues aimed to address the inconsistencies and concerns of many of the flow-related models and studies, and proposed a framework that differentiated the flow antecedents and experiential dimensions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Norsworthy |first1=Cameron |last2=Jackson |first2=Ben |last3=Dimmock |first3=James A. |date=August 2021 |title=Advancing our understanding of psychological flow: A scoping review of conceptualizations, measurements, and applications. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/bul0000337 |journal=Psychological Bulletin |language=en |volume=147 |issue=8 |pages=806–827 |doi=10.1037/bul0000337 |pmid=34898235 |issn=1939-1455|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Norsworthy et al. identified a core experience of flow including overarching antecedent constructs:

# Optimal challenge: A perceived capability to meet the challenging demands of the situation
# High motivation: A high motivational force

And recurring characteristics of the flow experience itself included:

# Absorption: A state of absorption in the task characterized by focused, undistracted attention, and a merging of action and awareness
# Effort-less control: A high sense of control in which the task feels less effortful than is typical for that person, characterized by fluidity of performance and an absence of concern over losing control
# Intrinsic reward: An intrinsically rewarding experience characterized by positive valence and optimal levels of arousal

The proposed definition of flow: Flow is an intrinsically rewarding state of absorption in a task in which a high degree of control feels more effort-less than normal.

==Mechanism==
In any given moment, a great deal of information is made available to each individual. Psychologists have found that one's mind can attend to only a certain amount of information at a time. According to Csikszentmihályi's 2004 [[TED (conference)|TED]] talk, that number is about "110 [[baud|bits of information per second]]."<ref name="McGuinness_2009">{{cite web | vauthors = McGuinness M |date=2009-02-16 |title=Mihaly Csikszentmihályi – Does Creativity Make You Happy? |website=Lateral Access |url=http://lateralaction.com/articles/mihaly-csikszentmihalyi/ |access-date=6 April 2015}}</ref> That may seem like a lot of information, but simple daily tasks take quite a lot of information. Just decoding speech takes about 40–60 bits of information per second,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Reed C, Durlach N |title=Note on Information Transfer Rates in Human Communication |journal=Presence |date=October 1998 |volume=7 |issue=5 |pages=509–518 |doi=10.1162/105474698565893 |s2cid=37035440 }}</ref> which is why when having a conversation, one cannot focus as much [[attention]] on other things.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Björkman |first=Beyza |date=2018-08-28 |title="This is not familiar to most people": navigating peer reviewers' comments and knowledge construction practices by PhD students in supervision interactions |journal=Journal of English as a Lingua Franca |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=333–354 |doi=10.1515/jelf-2018-0018 |s2cid=188378502 |issn=2191-933X|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Generally, people have the ability to decide what they will give their full attention to. This excludes basic distinctive feelings, such as hunger and pain.  However, when one is in the flow state, they are completely engrossed with the one task at hand and, without making the conscious decision to do so, lose awareness of all other things: time, people, distractions, and even basic bodily needs.<ref>{{Citation | mode=cs1 |type = preprint |last=Ergas |first=Oren |date=2017-09-02 |title=Attention please: Positioning attention at the center of curriculum and pedagogy |doi=10.31231/osf.io/mvfrw }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Salzen |first=Eric A. |date=August 2002 |title=The feeling of pain and the emotion of distress |journal=Behavioral and Brain Sciences |volume=25 |issue=4 |page=471 |doi=10.1017/s0140525x02380087 |s2cid=143866002 |issn=0140-525X}}</ref> According to Csikszentmihályi, this event occurs because all of the attention of the person in the flow state is on the task at hand; there is no more attention to be allocated.<ref name="Csikszentmihályi_1998">{{cite book | vauthors = Csikszentmihályi M |author-link=Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi |title=Optimal experience: psychological studies of flow in consciousness |chapter=The flow experience and its significance for human psychology |pages=15–35 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |place=Cambridge, UK |year=1988|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lNt6bdfoyxQC&q=The%20flow%20experience%20and%20its%20significance%20for%20human%20psychology&pg=PA15 |isbn=978-0-521-43809-4}}</ref>

The flow state has been described by Csikszentmihályi as the "optimal experience" in that one gets to a level of high gratification from the experience.<ref name= "Csikszentmihályi_1990">{{cite book | vauthors = Csikszentmihályi M |author-link1=Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi | publisher = Harper and Row |year=1990 |title=FLOW: The Psychology of Optimal Experience |url=http://www.psy-flow.com/sites/psy-flow/files/docs/flow.pdf |access-date=2 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150225201519/http://www.psy-flow.com/sites/psy-flow/files/docs/flow.pdf |archive-date=25 February 2015 |isbn=978-0-06-016253-5}}</ref> Achieving this experience is considered to be personal and "depends on the ability" of the individual.<ref name="Csikszentmihályi_1990"/> One's capacity and desire to overcome challenges in order to achieve their ultimate goals leads not only to the optimal experience but also to a sense of [[life satisfaction]] overall.<ref name="Csikszentmihályi_1990"/>

=== Operationalizing flow ===
Despite the attraction of flow and the varying flow interventions (e.g., mindfulness, goal-setting, visualisation) there has existed no gold standard intervention to promote flow experiences. Recently, Norsworthy et al. found continued evidence that it may be possible to 'train' flow through an educational intervention of flow.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Norsworthy |first1=C. |last2=Thelwell |first2=R. |last3=Weston |first3=N. |last4=A. Jackson |first4=S. |title=Flow training, flow states, and performance in elite athletes |url=http://www.ijsp-online.com/abstract/view/49/134 |journal=International Journal of Sport Psychology |date=2018 |volume=49 |issue=2 |pages=134–152 |doi=10.7352/ijsp.2018.49.134}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Norsworthy |first1=Cameron |last2=Dimmock |first2=James A. |last3=Nicholas |first3=Joanna |last4=Krause |first4=Amanda |last5=Jackson |first5=Ben |date=2023-12-01 |title=Psychological Flow Training: Feasibility and Preliminary Efficacy of an Educational Intervention on Flow |journal=International Journal of Applied Positive Psychology |language=en |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=531–554 |doi=10.1007/s41042-023-00098-2 |issn=2364-5059 |pmc=10204032 |pmid=37361627}}</ref>

==Measurement==
There are three common ways to measure flow experiences: the flow questionnaire (FQ), the experience sampling method (ESM), and the "standardized scales of the componential approach."<ref name="Moneta_2012">{{cite book | vauthors = Moneta G | veditors = Engeser S |year=2012 |title=Advances in Flow Research |chapter=On the Measurement and Conceptualization of Flow |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4614-2358-4}}</ref>

===Flow questionnaire===
The FQ requires individuals to identify definitions of flow and situations in which they believe that they have experienced flow, followed by a section that asks them to evaluate their personal experiences in these flow-inducing situations. The FQ identifies flow as multiple constructs, therefore allowing the results to be used to estimate differences in the likelihood of experiencing flow across a variety of factors. Another strength of the FQ is that it does not assume that everyone's flow experiences are the same. Because of this, the FQ is the ideal measure for estimating the prevalence of flow.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tse |first1=Dwight C. K. |last2=Nakamura |first2=Jeanne |last3=Csikszentmihalyi |first3=Mihaly |date=2022-08-01 |title=Flow Experiences Across Adulthood: Preliminary Findings on the Continuity Hypothesis |journal=Journal of Happiness Studies |language=en |volume=23 |issue=6 |pages=2517–2540 |doi=10.1007/s10902-022-00514-5 |s2cid=247257487 |issn=1573-7780|doi-access=free }}</ref> However, the FQ has some weaknesses that more recent methods have set out to address. The FQ does not allow for a measurement of the intensity of flow during specific activities. This method also does not measure the influence of the ratio of challenge to skill on the flow state.<ref name="Moneta_2012"/>

===Experience sampling method===
The ESM requires individuals to fill out the experience sampling form (ESF) at eight randomly chosen time intervals throughout the day. The purpose of this is to understand subjective experiences by estimating the time intervals that individuals spend in specific states during everyday life. The ESF is made up of 13 categorical items and 29 scaled items. The purpose of the categorical items is to determine the context and [[motivation]]al aspects of the current actions (these items include: time, location, companionship/desire for companionship, activity being performed, reason for performing activity). Because these are [[open-ended question]]s, the answers need to be coded by researchers. This needs to be done carefully so as to avoid any biases in the statistical analysis. The scaled items are intended to measure the levels of a variety of subjective feelings that the individual may be experiencing. The ESM is more complex than the FQ and contributes to understanding how flow plays out in a variety of situations. However, the possible biases make it a risky choice.<ref name="Moneta_2012"/>

===Standardized scales===

Jackson and colleagues<ref name="Jackson1996">{{Cite journal |last1=Jackson |first1=Susan A. |last2=Marsh |first2=Herbert W. |date=1996 |title=Development and validation of a scale to measure optimal experience: The Flow State Scale |journal=Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=17–35 |doi=10.1123/jsep.18.1.17}}</ref><ref name="Jackson2002">{{Cite journal |last1=Jackson |first1=Susan A. |last2=Eklund |first2=Robert C. |date=2002 |title=Assessing flow in physical activity: The Flow State Scale-2 and Dispositional Flow Scale-2 |journal=Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=133–150 |doi=10.1123/jsep.24.2.133}}</ref><ref name="Jackson2008a">{{Cite journal |last1=Jackson |first1=Susan A. |last2=Martin |first2=Andrew J. |last3=Eklund |first3=Robert C. |date=2008 |title=Long and Short Measures of Flow: Examining Construct Validity of the FSS-2, DFS-2 and New Brief Counterparts |journal=Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology |volume=30 |issue=5 |pages=561–587 |doi=10.1123/jsep.30.5.561 |pmid=18971512 }}</ref><ref name="Martin2008">{{Cite journal |last1=Martin |first1=Andrew J. |last2=Jackson |first2=Susan A. |date=2008 |title=Brief Approaches to Assessing Task Absorption and Enhanced Subjective Experience: Examining 'Short' and 'Core' Flow in Diverse Performance Domains |journal=Motivation and Emotion |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=141–157 |doi=10.1007/s11031-008-9094-0}}</ref><ref name="FlowManual2010">{{Cite book |last1=Jackson |first1=Susan A. |last2=Eklund |first2=Robert C. |last3=Martin |first3=Andrew J. |title=The FLOW Manual |publisher=Mind Garden, Inc. |year=2010 |doi=10.1037/t06469-000}}</ref> have created several scales that have been proven to be psychometrically valid and reliable: the Flow State Scale-2 (FSS-2)<ref name="Jackson1996" /><ref name="Jackson2002" /><ref name="Jackson2008a" /><ref name="FlowManual2010" /> (which measures flow as a state), and the Dispositional Flow Scale-2 (DFS-2)<ref name="Jackson1996" /><ref name="Jackson2002" /><ref name="Jackson2008a" /><ref name="FlowManual2010" /> (designed to measure flow as a trait, either general or domain-specific), being the most widely known. The statistical analysis of the DFS-2 and FSS-2 scales gives a more complete understanding of flow from a dimensional perspective than the ESM or the FQ.<ref name="Moneta2012">{{Cite book |last=Moneta |first=Giovanni B. |year=2012 |chapter=On the Measurement and Conceptualization of Flow |editor-last=Engeser |editor-first=Stefan |title=Advances in Flow Research |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4614-2358-4}}</ref> Jackson and colleagues also created short versions of the FSS-2 and DFS-2, and an additional brief scale that assesses the subjective experience of flow, called the Core Flow Scales.<ref name="Martin2008" /><ref name="FlowManual2010" /> More recently, the Psychological Flow Scale (PFS) that was designed to be used across domains and scientific disciplines was validated and offers a parsimonious alternative model of flow.<ref name="PFS2023">{{Cite journal |last1=Norsworthy |first1=Cameron |last2=Dimmock |first2=James A. |last3=Miller |first3=Daniel J. |last4=Krause |first4=Amanda |last5=Jackson |first5=Ben |date=2023-08-01 |title=Psychological Flow Scale (PFS): Development and Preliminary Validation of a New Flow Instrument that Measures the Core Experience of Flow to Reflect Recent Conceptual Advancements |journal=International Journal of Applied Positive Psychology |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=309–337 |doi=10.1007/s41042-023-00092-8 |issn=2364-5059 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Characteristics==
{{Mental state}}
The flow state can be entered while performing any activity; however, it is more likely to occur when the task or activity is wholeheartedly engaged for [[Motivation#Types of motivation|intrinsic purposes]].<ref name="Csikszentmihályi_1998"/><ref name="Snyder_2007">{{cite book | vauthors = Snyder CR, Lopez SJ |year=2007 |title=Positive psychology: The scientific and practical explorations of human strengths |publisher=Sage Publications |location=London, UK}}</ref> Passive activities such as taking a bath or even watching TV usually do not elicit a flow experience because active engagement is prerequisite to entering the flow state.<ref name="Csikszentmihalyi_1977">{{cite journal | vauthors = Csikszentmihalyi M, Larson R, Prescott S | title = The ecology of adolescent activity and experience | journal = Journal of Youth and Adolescence | volume = 6 | issue = 3 | pages = 281–94 | date = September 1977 | pmid = 24408457 | doi = 10.1007/BF02138940 | s2cid = 23892740 }}</ref><ref name="Delle_2000">{{cite journal | vauthors = Delle Fave A, Bassi M | title = The quality of experience in adolescents' daily lives: developmental perspectives | journal = Genetic, Social, and General Psychology Monographs | volume = 126 | issue = 3 | pages = 347–67 | date = August 2000 | pmid = 10950201 | doi = | url = }}</ref> While the activities that induce flow vary and may be multifaceted, Csikszentmihályi asserts that the experience of flow is similar whatever the activity.<ref name="Csikszentmihalyi_2000">{{cite journal | vauthors = Csikszentmihalyi M | title = Happiness, flow, and economic equality | journal = The American Psychologist | volume = 55 | issue = 10 | pages = 1163–4 | date = October 2000 | pmid = 11080848 | doi = 10.1037/0003-066X.55.10.1163| url = }}</ref>

Flow theory postulates that three conditions must be met to achieve flow:
# The activity must have clear goals and progress. This establishes structure and direction.<ref name="Csikszentmihályi_2005">{{cite book | vauthors = Csikszentmihályi M, Abuhamdeh S, Nakamura J |author-link1=Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi | veditors = Elliot A |year=2005 |title=Handbook of Competence and Motivation |chapter=Flow |publisher=The Guilford Press |location=New York |pages=598–698}}</ref>
# The task must provide clear and immediate feedback. This helps to negotiate any changing demands and allows adjusting performance to maintain the flow state.<ref name="Csikszentmihályi_2005"/>
# Good balance is required between the ''perceived'' challenges of the task and one's ''perceived'' skills. Confidence in the ability to complete the task is required.<ref name="Csikszentmihályi_2005"/>

It has been argued that the antecedent factors of flow are interrelated, and as such, a balance between perceived challenges and skills requires that the goals are clear and feedback is effective. Thus, such balance can be identified as the central precondition of flow experience.<ref name="Keller_2012">{{cite book | vauthors = Keller J, Landhäußer A | veditors = Engeser S |year=2012 |title=Advances in Flow Research |chapter=The Flow Model Revisited |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4614-2358-4 |pages=51–64 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-2359-1_3}}</ref>

In 1987, Massimini, Csíkszentmihályi and Carli published the eight-channel (or eight-sector) model of flow.<ref name="Massimini_1987">{{cite journal | vauthors = Massimini F, Csikszentmihalyi M, Carli M | title = The monitoring of optimal experience. A tool for psychiatric rehabilitation | journal = The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease | volume = 175 | issue = 9 | pages = 545–9 | date = September 1987 | pmid = 3655780 | doi = 10.1097/00005053-198709000-00006 }}</ref> (See Figure.) Antonella Delle Fave, who worked with Fausto Massimini at the [[University of Milan]], calls this graph the Experience Fluctuation Model.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Delle Fave A, Massimini F, Bassi M | title = Psychological Selection and Optimal Experience Across Cultures | chapter = Work: A Paradox in Flow Research | series = Cross-Cultural Advancements in Positive Psychology | date = 2011 | pages = 155–175 | publisher = Springer Science & Business Media | location = Dordrecht | volume = 2 | doi = 10.1007/978-90-481-9876-4_8 | isbn = 978-90-481-9875-7 | chapter-url = https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-90-481-9876-4_8 }}</ref> The model depicts the channels of experience that result from different levels of perceived challenges and perceived skills. The graph illustrates another aspect of flow: it is more likely to occur when the activity is a higher-than-average challenge (above the center point) and the individual has above-average skills (to the right of the center point).<ref name="Csikszentmihályi_1998"/> The center of the graph where the sectors meet represents the average level of challenge and skill across all individual daily activities. The further from the center an experience is, the greater the intensity of that state of being, whether it is flow or anxiety or boredom or relaxation.<ref name="Snyder_2007"/>

Several problems of the model have been discussed in the literature.<ref name="Keller_2012"/><ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Moneta GB | chapter = On the measurement and conceptualization of flow. | veditors = Engeser S | title = Advances in flow research | date = 2012 | pages = 23–50 | publisher = Springer | location = New York, NY }}</ref> One is that it does not ensure the perceived balance between challenges and skills, which is said to be the central precondition of flow experience. Individuals with a low average level of skills and a high average level of challenges (or the converse) do not necessarily experience a match between skills and challenges when both are above their individual average.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ellis GD, Voelkl JE, Morris C | title = Measurement and analysis issues with explanation of variance in daily experience using the flow model. | journal = Journal of Leisure Research | date = September 1994 | volume = 26 | issue = 4 | pages = 337–356 | doi = 10.1080/00222216.1994.11969966 | bibcode = 1994JLeiR..26..337E }}</ref> Another study found that low challenge situations which were surpassed by skill were associated with enjoyment, relaxation, and happiness, which, they claim, is contrary to flow theory.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Haworth J, Evans S |date=June 1995 |title=Challenge, skill and positive subjective states in the daily life of a sample of YTS students. |journal=Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology |doi=10.1111/j.2044-8325.1995.tb00576.x |volume=68 |issue=2 |pages=109–121}}</ref>

Schaffer (2013) proposed seven flow conditions:
# Knowing what to do
# Knowing how to do it
# Knowing how well one is doing
# Knowing where to go (if navigation is involved)
# High perceived challenges
# High perceived skills
# Freedom from distractions

Schaffer published a flow condition questionnaire (FCQ), to measure each of these seven flow conditions for any given task or activity.<ref name="Schaffer_2013">{{citation | vauthors = Schaffer O |year=2013 |title=Crafting Fun User Experiences: A Method to Facilitate Flow |publisher=Human Factors International |url=http://humanfactors.com/funexperiences.asp}}</ref>

===Challenges to maintaining flow===
Some of the challenges to staying in flow include states of [[apathy]], [[boredom]], and [[anxiety]]. The state of apathy is characterized by easy challenges and low skill level requirements, resulting in a general lack of interest in the activity. Boredom is a slightly different state that occurs when challenges are few, but one's skill level exceeds those challenges causing one to seek higher challenges. A state of anxiety occurs when challenges are high enough to exceed perceived skill level, causing distress and uneasiness. These states in general prevent achieving the balance necessary for flow.<ref name = "Nakamura_2005">{{cite journal | vauthors = Nakamura J, Csikszentmihályi M |author-link2=Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi |year=2005 |title=The concept of flow |journal=Handbook of Positive Psychology |pages=89–105}}</ref> Csíkszentmihályi has said, "If challenges are too low, one gets back to flow by increasing them. If challenges are too great, one can return to the flow state by learning new skills."<ref name="Cherry_2014"/>

===The autotelic personality===
Csíkszentmihályi hypothesized that people with certain personality traits may be better able to achieve flow than the average person. These traits include curiosity, persistence, low [[egotism]], and a high propensity to perform activities for intrinsic reasons. People with most of these personality traits are said to have an ''autotelic personality'', i.e. a disposition to actively seek challenges and flow experiences.<ref name="Snyder_2007"/><ref>{{cite book |last=Baumann |first=Nicola |title=Advances in Flow Research |chapter=Autotelic Personality |publisher=Springer New York |publication-place=New York, NY |date=2012 |isbn=978-1-4614-2358-4 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-2359-1_9 |pages=165–186}}</ref> The term "autotelic" derives from two [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] words, ''autos'' ("self") and ''telos'' ("end" or "goal").

There is scant research on the ''autotelic personality'', but results of the few studies that have been conducted suggest that indeed some people are more likely to experience flow than others. One researcher (Abuhamdeh, 2000) found that people with an autotelic personality have a greater preference for "high-action-opportunity, high-skills situations that stimulate them and encourage growth" compared to those without an autotelic personality.<ref name="Snyder_2007"/> It is in such high-challenge, high-skills situations that people are most likely to experience flow.

Experimental evidence shows that a balance between individual skills and demands of the task (compared to boredom and overload) only elicits the flow experience in individuals having an internal [[locus of control]]<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Keller J, Blomann F | title = Locus of control and the flow experience: An experimental analysis. | journal = European Journal of Personality | date = November 2008 | volume = 22 | issue = 7 | pages = 589–607 | doi = 10.1002/per.692 | s2cid = 145112668 }}</ref> or a habitual action orientation.<ref name="Keller_2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Keller J, Bless H | title = Flow and regulatory compatibility: an experimental approach to the flow model of intrinsic motivation | journal = Personality & Social Psychology Bulletin | volume = 34 | issue = 2 | pages = 196–209 | date = February 2008 | pmid = 18212330 | doi = 10.1177/0146167207310026 | s2cid = 12583021 }}</ref> Several correlational studies found [[need for achievement]] to be a personal characteristic that fosters flow experiences.<ref name="Engeser_2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Engeser S, Rheinberg F | title = Flow, performance and moderators of challenge-skill balance. | journal = Motivation and Emotion | date = September 2008 | volume = 32 | issue = 3 | pages = 158–72 | doi = 10.1007/s11031-008-9102-4 | s2cid = 14745590 }}</ref><ref name="Schüler_2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Schüler J | title = Arousal of flow experience in a learning setting and its effects on exam performance and affect. | journal = Zeitschrift für Pädagogische Psychologie | date = January 2007 | volume = 21 | issue = 3–4 | pages = 217–227 | doi = 10.1024/1010-0652.21.3.217 | url = http://nbn-resolving.de/urn:nbn:de:bsz:352-0-382895 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Eisenberger R, Jones JR, Stinglhamber F, Shanock L, Randall AT | title = Flow experiences at work: For high need achievers alone? | journal = Journal of Organizational Behavior | date = November 2005 | volume = 26 | issue = 7 | pages = 755–75 | doi = 10.1002/job.337 }}</ref>

Autotelic Personality also has been shown in studies to correlate and show overlapping of flow in personal life and the [[Big Five personality traits|Big Five Personality Traits]] of Extraversion, Agreeableness, [[Conscientiousness]], Neuroticism, and Openness to Experience, especially the traits of agreeableness and extraversion. Study of Autotelic Personality is difficult as most studies are performed through self-evaluation,  a [[Big_Five_personality_traits#Limitations_of_self-report|recognized difficulty]] for Big Five questionnaires.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ross |first1=Scott R. |last2=Keiser |first2=Heidi N. |date=March 2014 |title=Autotelic personality through a five-factor lens: Individual differences in flow-propensity |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0191886913012853 |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |language=en |volume=59 |pages=3–8 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2013.09.029|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Marty-Dugas |first1=Jeremy |last2=Smilek |first2=Daniel |date=November 2019 |title=Deep, effortless concentration: re-examining the flow concept and exploring relations with inattention, absorption, and personality |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00426-018-1031-6 |journal=Psychological Research |language=en |volume=83 |issue=8 |pages=1760–1777 |doi=10.1007/s00426-018-1031-6 |pmid=29948186 |hdl=10012/15237 |s2cid=49433053 |issn=0340-0727|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Group==
{{see also|Crowd psychology}}

More than one type of flow exists. Group flow (or '''team flow''') is notably different from independent flow, as it is inherently mutual. Group flow is attainable when the performance unit is a group, such as a team or musical group. When groups cooperate to agree on goals and patterns, social flow, commonly known as group cohesion, is much more likely to occur. If a group still has not entered flow, a team-level challenge may stimulate the group to harmonize.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Walker CJ | title =  Experiencing flow: Is doing it together better than doing it alone? | journal = The Journal of Positive Psychology | date = January 2010 | volume = 5 | issue = 1 | pages = 3–11 | doi = 10.1080/17439760903271116 | s2cid = 143476331 }}</ref> Group flow is different from synchronized solitary flow, in which a group is simultaneously experiencing individual flow. Group Flow occurs in an interpersonal manner, in which the act of others being present is inherent to the cause of the state of flow.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Pels |first1=Fabian |last2=Kleinert |first2=Jens |last3=Mennigen |first3=Florian |date=2018-12-31 |title=Group flow: A scoping review of definitions, theoretical approaches, measures and findings |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=13 |issue=12 |article-number=e0210117 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0210117 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=6312318 |pmid=30596773 |bibcode=2018PLoSO..1310117P |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In research presented in a review written by [[PLOS One|PLoS ONE]],<ref name=":0" /> Pels ''et al.'' stated, "Group contexts introduce many additional variables that cause individuals to act, think, and feel differently during group situations compared to solitary situations." Due to these additional variables, the cause and effect of flow are vastly different and unique to the experience of individual flow, hence providing evidence for the existence of a separate flow state: group flow.

=== Physiology of group flow ===
Snijdewint<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Snijdewint |first1=Joyce A. |last2=Scheepers |first2=Daan |date=May 2023 |title=Group-based flow: The influence of cardiovascular synchronization and identifiability |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/psyp.14227 |journal=Psychophysiology |language=en |volume=60 |issue=5 |article-number=e14227 |doi=10.1111/psyp.14227 |pmid=36458474 |hdl=1887/3514137 |s2cid=254149712 |issn=0048-5772|hdl-access=free }}</ref> studies the correlation of the physiological effect of a group that simultaneously reports a "flow" state. This research concludes that between many similar studies when a participant reports a feeling of flow state (in synchronization or due to a group environment), there are similarities in the cardiovascular triggers<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Scheepers |first1=Daan |last2=Keller |first2=Johannes |date=2022 |title=On the physiology of flow: Bridging flow theory with the biopsychosocial model of challenge and threat |journal=International Journal of Psychophysiology |volume=182 |issue=182 |pages=119–128|doi=10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2022.10.007 |pmid=36273715 |s2cid=253057327 |hdl=1887/3513836 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> that the participants experience'''.'''

==Applications==

===Applications suggested by Csíkszentmihályi versus other practitioners===
Only Csíkszentmihályi seems to have published suggestions for [[extrinsic]] applications of the flow concept, such as [[design]] methods for playgrounds to elicit the flow experience. Other practitioners of Csíkszentmihályi's flow concept focus on [[intrinsic and extrinsic properties (philosophy)|intrinsic]] applications, such as [[spirituality]], [[performance improvement]], or [[self-help]].

===Education===
{{Essay-like|section|date=August 2023}}
Flow state theory suggests that when individuals are in a state of flow, they experience deep immersion, focus, and intrinsic motivation in their activities.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Borovay |first1=Lindsay A. |last2=Shore |first2=Bruce M. |last3=Caccese |first3=Christina |last4=Yang |first4=Ethan |last5=Hua |first5=Olivia (Liv) |date=February 2019 |title=Flow, Achievement Level, and Inquiry-Based Learning |journal=Journal of Advanced Academics |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=74–106|doi=10.1177/1932202X18809659 |s2cid=149756416 |doi-access=free }}</ref> In the context of education, flow has been associated with increased [[student engagement]].

Numerous studies have examined the relationship between flow and student engagement, demonstrating positive associations. For example, Csikszentmihalyi and Larson (1984) found that students who reported experiencing flow during their academic tasks exhibited higher levels of engagement, concentration, and enjoyment. Similarly, Cho and Lee (2017) discovered that flow experiences positively correlated with student engagement in a college classroom setting.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Oliveira |first1=Wilk |last2=Tenório |first2=Kamilla |last3=Hamari |first3=Juho |last4=Pastushenko |first4=Olena |last5=Isotani |first5=Seiji |date=11 November 2021 |title=Predicting students' flow experience through behavior data in gamified educational systems |journal=Smart Learning Environments |volume=8 |issue=1 |page=30|doi=10.1186/s40561-021-00175-6 |s2cid=256401181 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Flow state research has also explored its impact on learning outcomes, such as [[knowledge acquisition]], skill development, and creativity. When students are in a state of flow, they are more likely to experience a heightened sense of focus, concentration, and [[Motivation|intrinsic motivation]], which may lead to improved [[Educational aims and objectives|learning outcomes]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gyllenpalm |first1=Jakob |date=1 June 2018 |title=Inquiry and flow in science education |journal=Cultural Studies of Science Education |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=429–435|doi=10.1007/s11422-016-9794-9 |bibcode=2018CSSE...13..429G |s2cid=255162908 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Studies have shown that flow experiences can enhance cognitive processes related to learning. For instance, Schüler and Brunner (2009) found that university students who reported being in a state of flow while studying demonstrated better [[Recall (memory)|information recall]] and [[Problem solving|problem-solving abilities]]. In addition, studies by Simons and Dewitte (2004) and Jackson and Csikszentmihalyi (1999) revealed that flow experiences positively influenced creativity and innovation among students.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

==== Applications ====
The concept of flow has been applied to various educational settings and practices, offering valuable insights for teaching and learning. Here are a few notable applications:
* Skill development: Flow state theory can inform the design of [[Curriculum|curricula]] and learning activities that promote the development of specific skills.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Peifer |first1=Corinna |last2=Wolters |first2=Gina |last3=Harmat |first3=László |last4=Heutte |first4=Jean |last5=Tan |first5=Jasmine |last6=Freire |first6=Teresa |last7=Tavares |first7=Dionísia |last8=Fonte |first8=Carla |last9=Andersen |first9=Frans Orsted |last10=van den Hout |first10=Jef |last11=Šimleša |first11=Milija |last12=Pola |first12=Linda |last13=Ceja |first13=Lucia |last14=Triberti |first14=Stefano |date=2022 |title=A Scoping Review of Flow Research |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |volume=13|article-number=815665 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2022.815665 |pmid=35465560 |pmc=9022035 |doi-access=free }}</ref> By structuring tasks to align with students' skill levels and providing immediate feedback, educators can facilitate skill acquisition and mastery.
* Optimal [[learning environment]]s: Flow state research suggests that the design of learning environments can significantly impact student engagement and learning outcomes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rodríguez-Ardura |first1=Inma |last2=Meseguer-Artola |first2=Antoni |date=June 2017 |title=Flow in e-learning: What drives it and why it matters: Flow in e-learning: what drives it and why it matters |journal=British Journal of Educational Technology |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=899–915 |doi=10.1111/bjet.12480 |hdl=10609/53181 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Creating environments that are challenging, supportive, and tailored to students' interests can facilitate flow experiences and foster deep learning.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}
* [[Motivation]] and [[well-being]]: Flow state theory emphasizes the role of intrinsic motivation in optimal performance and well-being. Educators can encourage students' intrinsic motivation by promoting [[autonomy]], competence, and relatedness in the learning process, thus facilitating flow experiences.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wagner |first1=L |last2=Holenstein |first2=M |last3=Wepf |first3=H |last4=Ruch |first4=W |date=2020 |title=Character Strengths Are Related to Students' Achievement, Flow Experiences, and Enjoyment in Teacher-Centered Learning, Individual, and Group Work Beyond Cognitive Ability. |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |volume=11 |article-number=1324 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01324 |pmid=32765332 |pmc=7378955 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* [[Classroom management]]: Understanding flow state dynamics can help educators manage classroom activities more effectively.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Karwowski |first1=M |date=June 2018 |title=The Flow of Learning. |journal=Europe's Journal of Psychology |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=291–295 |doi=10.5964/ejop.v14i2.1660 |pmid=30008947 |pmc=6016036 }}</ref> By providing clear instructions, structuring tasks, and offering appropriate challenges, educators can create conditions conducive to flow, leading to improved classroom experiences.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

These applications demonstrate the potential benefits of integrating flow state theory into educational practices. However, further research is needed to explore the specific strategies and [[Intervention (counseling)|interventions]] that effectively foster flow in educational settings.[[File:South-Goodwin.jpg|thumb|250px|Young child, painting a model]]

==== History ====
In [[education]], the concept of [[overlearning]] plays a role in a student's ability to achieve flow. Csíkszentmihályi<ref name= "Csikszentmihályi_1990" /> states that overlearning enables the mind to concentrate on visualizing the desired performance as a singular, integrated action instead of a set of actions. Challenging assignments that (slightly) stretch one's skills lead to flow.<ref name=PP11>{{citation | vauthors = Snyder CR, Lopez SJ |name-list-style=amp  |author-link1=C. R. Snyder |year=2007 |title=Positive Psychology |publisher=Sage Publications, Inc. |chapter=11 |isbn=978-0-7619-2633-7}}</ref>

In the 1950s British cybernetician [[Gordon Pask]] designed an adaptive teaching machine called SAKI, an early example of "e-learning". The machine is discussed in some detail in Stafford Beer's book "Cybernetics and Management".<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Beer S |year=1967 |title=Cybernetics and Management |publisher=The English Universities Press |isbn=978-0-340-04594-7}}</ref> In the patent application for SAKI (1956),<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Pask G |title=US patent 2984017 A: Apparatus for assisting an operator in performing a skill |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US2984017}}</ref> Pask's comments (some of which are included below) indicate an awareness of the pedagogical importance of balancing student competence with didactic challenge, which is quite consistent with flow theory:

{{blockquote|If the operator is receiving data at too slow a rate, he is likely to become bored and attend to other irrelevant data.

If the data given indicates too precisely what responses the operator is required to make, the skill becomes too easy to perform and the operator again tends to become bored.

If the data given is too complicated or is given at too great a rate, the operator is unable to deal with it. He is then liable to become discouraged and lose interest in performing or learning the skill.

Ideally, for an operator to perform a skill efficiently, the data presented to him should always be of sufficient complexity to maintain his interest and maintain a competitive situation, but not so complex as to discourage the operator. Similarly these conditions should obtain at each stage of a learning process if it is to be efficient. A tutor teaching one pupil seeks to maintain just these conditions.}}

Around 2000, it came to the attention of Csíkszentmihályi that the principles and practices of the [[Montessori Method]] of education seemed to purposefully set up continuous flow opportunities and experiences for students. Csíkszentmihályi and psychologist Kevin Rathunde embarked on a multi-year study of student experiences in Montessori settings and traditional educational settings. The research supported observations that students achieved flow experiences more frequently in Montessori settings.<ref>{{citation | vauthors = Rathunde K, Csikszetnmihályi M |journal=American Journal of Education |title=Middle school students' motivation and quality of experience: A comparison of Montessori and traditional school environments |issue=3 |volume=111 |pages=341–371 |year=2005 |doi=10.1086/428885|s2cid=146766889 }}</ref><ref>{{citation | vauthors = Rathunde K, Csikszentmihályi M |author-link2=Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi |title=The social context of middle school: Teachers, friends, and activities in Montessori and traditional school environments |journal=Elementary School Journal |volume=106 |issue=1 |pages=59–79 |year=2005 |doi=10.1086/496907|s2cid=145336225 }}</ref><ref>{{cite conference | vauthors = Rathunde K, Csikszentmihályi M |author-link2=Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi |title=The developing person: An experiential perspective | veditors = Lerner RM, Damon W |series=Handbook of Child Psychology |book-title=Theoretical models of human development |issue=1 |edition=6 |place=New York |publisher=Wiley |year=2006}}</ref>

===Music===
Musicians, especially [[Musical improvisation|improvisational]] [[solo (music)|soloists]], may experience a state of flow while playing their instrument.<ref>{{citation | vauthors = Parncutt R, McPherson GE |title=The Science & Psychology of Music Performance: Creative Strategies for Teaching and Learning Book |publisher=Oxford University Press US |page=119 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NCySp2NzAm8C&q=improvisation+flow+Cs%C3%ADkszentmih%C3%A1lyi&pg=PA119 |access-date=2009-02-07 |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-19-513810-8}}</ref>
Research has shown that performers in a flow state have a heightened quality of performance as opposed to when they are not in a flow state.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=O'Neill|first=Susan|date=1999|title=Flow Theory and the Development of Musical Performance Skills|journal=Bulletin of the Council for Research in Music Education|volume=141|issue=141|pages=129–134|jstor=40318998|via=University of Illinois Press}}</ref> In a study performed with professional classical pianists who played piano pieces several times to induce a flow state, a significant relationship was found between the flow state of the pianist and the pianist's heart rate, blood pressure, and major [[facial muscles]]. As the pianist entered the flow state, heart rate and blood pressure decreased, and the major facial muscles relaxed. This study further emphasized that flow is a state of effortless attention. In spite of the effortless attention and overall relaxation of the body, the performance of the pianist during the flow state improved.<ref name="de ManzanoTheorell2010">{{cite journal | vauthors = de Manzano O, Theorell T, Harmat L, Ullén F | title = The psychophysiology of flow during piano playing | journal = Emotion | volume = 10 | issue = 3 | pages = 301–311 | date = June 2010 | pmid = 20515220 | doi = 10.1037/a0018432 | s2cid = 13036396 }}</ref>

Groups of drummers go through a state of flow when they sense a collective energy that drives the beat, something they refer to as ''getting into the groove'' or [[Entrainment (biomusicology)|entrainment]]. Likewise, drummers and bass guitarists often describe a state of flow when they are feeling the downbeat together as being ''in the pocket.''<ref>{{cite web |vauthors=Elliott B |date=9 June 2003 |title=In The Pocket |website=www.drummercafe.com |language=en-GB |url=http://www.drummercafe.com/education/articles/in-the-pocket.html |access-date=2016-04-01 |archive-date=2012-04-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120421011112/http://www.drummercafe.com/education/articles/in-the-pocket.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Researchers have measured flow through subscales; challenge-skill balance, merging of action and awareness, clear goals, unambiguous feedback, total concentration, sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, transformation of time and autotelic experience.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Wrigley WJ, Emmerson SB | title = The experience of the flow state in live music performance. | journal = Psychology of Music | date = May 2013 | volume = 41 | issue = 3 | pages = 292–305 | doi = 10.1177/0305735611425903 | s2cid = 144877389 }}=</ref>

===Sports===
[[File:Concentration.jpg|thumb|Flow may occur in challenging sports such as [[eventing]].]]
The concept of ''being in the zone'' during an athletic performance fit within Csíkszentmihályi's description of the flow experience. Theories and applications of ''being in the zone'' and its relationship with an athletic competitive advantage are topics studied in the field of [[sport psychology]].<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Young JA, Pain MD |title=The Zone: Evidence of a Universal Phenomenon for Athletes Across Sports |work=Athletic Insight |url=http://www.athleticinsight.com/Vol1Iss3/Empirical_Zone.htm |access-date=2008-05-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180129145759/http://www.athleticinsight.com/Vol1Iss3/Empirical_Zone.htm |archive-date=2018-01-29 }}</ref> Flow experience has received considerable attention within sport psychology, with Jackson conducting qualitative research on the flow experience in elite athletes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jackson |first=S.A. |date=1992 |title=Athletes in flow: A qualitative investigation of flow states in elite figure skaters |journal=Journal of Applied Sport Psychology |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=161–180 |doi=10.1080/10413209208406459}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jackson |first=S.A. |date=1995 |title=Factors influencing the occurrence of flow in elite athletes |journal=Journal of Applied Sport Psychology |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=135–163 |doi=10.1080/10413209508406962}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jackson |first=S.A. |date=1996 |title=Toward a conceptual understanding of the flow experience in elite athletes |journal=Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport |volume=67 |issue=1 |pages=76–90 |doi=10.1080/02701367.1996.10607928 |pmid=8735997 }}</ref> Jackson co-authored with Csikszentmihalyi the book, ''Flow in Sports''.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Jackson |first1=S.A. |last2=Csikszentmihalyi |first2=M.C. |year=1999 |title=Flow in Sports: The Keys to Optimal Experiences and Performances |location=Champaign, IL |publisher=Human Kinetics |isbn=978-0-88011-876-7}}</ref> In a qualitative study of NCAA Division I athletes on the experience of flow, 94% of the athletes described flow state as causing a merging of action and awareness, and that it was effortless and automatic.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chavez |first=Edward J. |date=2008 |title=Flow in Sport: A Study of College Athletes |journal=Imagination, Cognition and Personality |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=69–91 |doi=10.2190/ic.28.1.f |s2cid=143685336 |issn=0276-2366}}</ref>

[[Timothy Gallwey]]'s influential works on the "inner game" of sports, such as [[golf]] and [[tennis]], described the mental coaching and attitudes required to "get in the zone" and fully internalize mastery of the sport.<ref>{{citation | vauthors = Galwey T |year=1976 |title=Inner Tennis&nbsp;— Playing the Game}}</ref>

Roy Palmer suggests that "being in the zone" may also influence movement patterns as better integration of the conscious and subconscious reflex functions improves coordination. Many athletes describe the effortless nature of their performance while achieving personal bests.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = King S |year=2006 |title=Running in the Zone A Handbook for Seasoned Athletes |publisher=Trafford Publishing |location=Victoria, BC Canada |isbn=978-1-4120-6857-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Locke A |date=2001-02-01 |title=Being in the zone: notions of agency in athletic performance |journal=Proceedings of the British Psychological Society |issn=1350-472X |volume=9 |issue=1 |page=83 |url=http://eprints.hud.ac.uk/7223/ |access-date=2016-04-01}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Jenkins L |date=May 20, 2015 |title=Stephen Curry's next stage: MVP has Warriors closing in on the NBA Finals |website=www.si.com |url=https://www.si.com/nba/2015/05/21/stephen-curry-mvp-golden-state-warriors-sports-illustrated-nba-playoffs |access-date=2016-04-01}}</ref>

Many [[martial arts]] such as Japanese [[budō]] contain aspects of psychological flow.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Henderson S |date=November 24, 2015 |title=Finding Your Inner Master – Kigatsuku |website=International Budo Institute |url=http://www.i-budo.com/zen-kata/ |access-date=21 September 2017}}</ref> [[Mixed martial arts]] champion and [[Karate]] master [[Lyoto Machida]] uses meditation techniques before fights to attain [[mushin (mental state)|mushin]], a concept that, by his description, is in all respects equal to flow.

[[Formula One]] driver [[Ayrton Senna]], during qualifying for the [[1988 Monaco Grand Prix]], explained: "I was already on pole, [...] and I just kept going. Suddenly I was nearly two seconds faster than anybody else, including my team mate with the same car. And suddenly I realised that I was no longer driving the car consciously. I was driving it by a kind of instinct, only I was in a different dimension. It was like I was in a tunnel."<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Donaldson G |date=May 23, 2019 |title=Senna's Magic Monaco Lap |url=http://www.f1speedwriter.com/2018/05/sennas-magic-monaco-lap.html |access-date=2020-12-23}}</ref>

Former [[Grand Prix motorcycle racing|500 GP]] rider [[Wayne Gardner]] talking about his victory at the [[1990 Australian motorcycle Grand Prix|1990 Australian Grand Prix]] on ''The Unrideables 2'' documentary said: "During these last five laps I had this sort of above body experience where actually raised up above and I could see myself racing. It was kind of a remote control and it's the weirdest thing I've ever had in my life. [...]" After the race [[Mick Doohan|Mick [Doohan]]] and in fact [[Wayne Rainey]] said: "How the hell did you do that?" and I said: "I have no idea."<ref>{{cite web |title=The Unrideables 2 |url=https://vimeo.com/92724437#t=1212s}}</ref>

===Religion and spirituality===
In [[Yoga|yogic]] traditions such as [[Raja Yoga]], reference is made to a state of ''flow''<ref>{{cite web |title=Yoga Sutras 3.9-3.16: Witnessing Subtle Transitions with Samyama |publisher=Swamij.com |url=http://www.swamij.com/yoga-sutras-30916.htm |access-date=2013-11-12}}</ref> in the practice of [[Samyama]], a psychological absorption in the object of meditation.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Sansonese JN |author-link=J. Nigro Sansonese |year=1994 |title=The Body of Myth: Mythology, Shamanic Trance, and the Sacred Geography of the Body |publisher=Inner Traditions |isbn=978-0-89281-409-1 |page=26 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aUZBqTKTAfIC&q=samyama+japan+koan&pg=PA26 |access-date=2009-03-06}}</ref>

===Games and gaming===

Flow in [[game]]s and gaming has been linked to the [[laws of learning]] as a part of the explanation for why learning-games (the use of games to introduce material, improve understanding, or increase retention) have the potential to be effective.<ref name= "Murphy_2011" >{{citation | vauthors = Murphy C |date=August 2011 |title=Why Games Work and the Science of Learning |url=http://www.goodgamesbydesign.com/Files/WhyGamesWork_TheScienceOfLearning_CMurphy_2011.pdf |access-date=October 7, 2021}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=October 2021|reason=Author claims on personal site to have intended to present at the 'Modsim World 2011' conference but the proceedings website for that shows no such paper or mention of author. I also found a claim it won an 'Best Tutorial' at I/ITSEC 2011 but again the proceedings webpage shows no such paper or mention of the author.}} In particular, flow is intrinsically motivating, which is a part of the law of readiness. The condition of feedback, required for flow, is associated with the feedback aspects of the law of exercise. This is exhibited in well designed games, in particular, where players perform at the edge of their competency as they are guided by clear goals and feedback.<ref name="Rutledge_2012"/> The positive emotions associated with flow are associated with the law of effect. The intense experiences of being in a state of flow are directly associated with the law of intensity. Thus, the experience of gaming can be so engaging and motivating as it meets many of the laws of learning, which are inextricably connected to creating flow.

In games often much can be achieved thematically through an imbalance between challenge level and skill level. Horror games often keep challenges significantly above the player's level of competency in order to foster a continual feeling of anxiety. Conversely, so called "relaxation games" keep the level of challenges significantly below the player's competency level, in order to achieve an opposite effect.<ref>{{Cite book |first=Lennart |last=Nacke |title=Boredom, Immersion, Flow a pilot study investigating player experience. |date=2008 |publisher=IADIS Press |oclc=1026876887}}</ref> The video game ''[[Flow (video game)|Flow]]'' was designed as part of [[Jenova Chen]]'s master's thesis for exploring the design decisions that allow players to achieve the flow state, by adjusting the difficulty dynamically during play.<ref name="Miller_2006">{{cite web | vauthors = Miller R |date=2006-09-18 |title=Joystiq interview: Jenova Chen |publisher=[[Joystiq]] |url=http://www.joystiq.com/2006/09/18/joystiq-qanda-jenova-chen/ |access-date=2011-01-05 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090102012220/http://www.joystiq.com/2006/09/18/joystiq-qanda-jenova-chen/ |archive-date=2009-01-02}}</ref>

It improves performance; calling the phenomenon "TV trance," a 1981 ''[[BYTE]]'' article discussed how "the best seem to enter a trance where they play but don't pay attention to the details of the game."<ref name="Smith_1981">{{cite news | vauthors = Smith T |date=December 1981 |title=The Game of Left/Right |work=BYTE |page=278 |url=https://archive.org/stream/byte-magazine-1981-12/1981_12_BYTE_06-12_Computer_Games#page/n279/mode/2up |access-date=29 January 2015}}</ref> The primary goal of games is to create entertainment through [[Motivation#Types of motivation|intrinsic motivation]], which is related to flow; that is, without intrinsic motivation it is virtually impossible to establish flow.<ref name="Lowry_2012">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lowry PB, Gaskin J, Twyman N, Hammer B, Roberts T | title = Taking 'fun and games' seriously: Proposing the hedonic-motivation system adoption model (HMSAM) | journal = Journal of the Association for Information Systems | date = November 2012 | volume = 14 | issue = 11 | pages = 617–71 | doi = 10.17705/1jais.00347 | ssrn = 2177442 | s2cid = 2810596 | url = https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2177442 | url-access = subscription }}</ref> Through the balance of skill and challenge, the player's brain is aroused, with attention engaged and motivation high.<ref name="Rutledge_2012">{{cite web | vauthors = Rutledge P |title=The Positive Side of Video Games: Part III |publisher=paper blog |url=http://en.paperblog.com/the-positive-side-of-video-games-part-iii-294723/ |access-date=2012-11-28}}</ref> Thus, the use of flow in games helps foster an enjoyable experience, which in turn increases motivation and draws players to continue playing. As such, game designers strive to integrate flow principles into their projects.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Chen J |title=Flow in Games |url=http://www.jenovachen.com/flowingames/introduction.htm |access-date=2008-05-16 |year=2008}}</ref> Overall, the experience of play is fluid and is intrinsically psychologically rewarding independent of scores or in-game successes in the flow state.<ref name="Rutledge_2012"/>

===Pain modulation===
Flow has recently been discussed as a psychological state potentially associated with modulation of pain perception, with emerging conceptual frameworks suggesting a possible reduction in pain during states of deep task engagement. This phenomenon, referred to as flow-induced analgesia, highlights the role of cognitive-emotional processes in central pain modulation.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Gromakovskis
 |first1=V
